slots.sample: trace_id alone isn't enough to join spans to logs safely. Clock skew and missing correlation IDs mean the join needs a time-window fallback.
slots.label: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm

slots.sample: The obvious way to correlate a log line with a span is matching trace_id. In practice, roughly 6% of log lines in a typical fleet don't carry a trace_id at all — older services, background jobs, or logs emitted just before context propagation kicks in. HelixQL's correlation join has to handle both cases.
slots.label: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm

slots.sample: The primary path: exact trace_id match
slots.label: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm

slots.sample: When both sides carry a trace_id, the join is a straightforward hash join as described elsewhere — build a hash table on spans keyed by trace_id, probe with log lines. This resolves the large majority of correlation queries and is the cheap, well-optimized path.
slots.label: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm

slots.sample: The fallback: time-window and process identity
slots.label: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm

slots.sample: For log lines without a trace_id, HelixQL can fall back to a soft join on service + pod/instance identity plus a time window bounded by the span's start and end timestamps, padded by a configurable skew tolerance (default 250ms to account for clock drift between hosts).
slots.label: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm

slots.sample: Why fuzzy joins are opt-in
slots.label: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm

slots.sample: A time-window join over a busy pod can match a log line to the wrong request if two spans on the same instance overlap tightly — we measured a false-positive attach rate around 3.8% under high concurrency (dozens of requests per pod per second). Because of that, HelixQL requires `kind=fuzzy` explicitly rather than silently falling back, and every fuzzy-joined row carries a `correlation_confidence` field so downstream consumers can filter low-confidence matches out.
slots.label: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm

slots.sample: Cost comparison
slots.label: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm

slots.sample: An exact trace_id join over a 10-minute window with 2.4M spans and 8.1M logs runs in about 340ms on our benchmark cluster. The fuzzy fallback over the same window, because it can't use the trace_id hash index and must scan time-ordered log ranges per pod, takes closer to 1.9s — a real cost, which is why it's reserved for the minority of logs that genuinely lack a trace_id.
slots.label: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm

slots.sample: Exact trace_id hash join handles the majority case and runs in the low hundreds of milliseconds.
slots.label: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm

slots.sample: Time-window fuzzy join is opt-in, tagged with a confidence score, and roughly 5-6x slower.
slots.label: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm

slots.sample: Default clock-skew tolerance is 250ms, tunable per pipeline.
slots.label: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm

slots.sample: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm
slots.label: Joining spans to logs: the trace_id and time-window algorithm

slots.sample: Raw 15-second resolution can't survive 13 months of retention economically. Here's how rollups are built, and how a query picks which one to read.
slots.label: Downsampling rollups and how the planner picks a resolution

slots.sample: Storing every 15-second metric point at full resolution for 13 months would be prohibitively expensive for most workloads. Helix builds progressively coarser rollups — 1 minute, 1 hour, 1 day — and the planner decides which one a query actually needs.
slots.label: Downsampling rollups and how the planner picks a resolution

slots.sample: How rollups are built
slots.label: Downsampling rollups and how the planner picks a resolution

slots.sample: A background compaction job aggregates raw chunks into 1-minute rollups (count, sum, min, max, and a handful of quantile estimates via t-digest) six hours after ingest, once the tail-based sampling and late-arrival windows have closed. 1-hour rollups are built from 1-minute rollups a day later, and 1-day rollups from those a week later — each pass roughly 15-20x smaller than its source.
slots.label: Downsampling rollups and how the planner picks a resolution

slots.sample: Resolution selection at query time
slots.label: Downsampling rollups and how the planner picks a resolution

slots.sample: The planner picks a resolution based on the requested time range and the visualization's effective pixel width, aiming for roughly 2-4 raw points per rendered pixel — enough to preserve the shape without transferring resolution the query can't display.
slots.label: Downsampling rollups and how the planner picks a resolution

slots.sample: Had that same query asked for `bin(timestamp, 15s)` over 90 days, the planner would reject it outright above a configurable row-count ceiling (default 2 million points) rather than silently scanning raw data for three months — a query that would otherwise touch on the order of 518 million raw points.
slots.label: Downsampling rollups and how the planner picks a resolution

slots.sample: The quantile problem
slots.label: Downsampling rollups and how the planner picks a resolution

slots.sample: Rolling up p95/p99 correctly is not as simple as averaging averages — you can't merge two p95 values into a valid combined p95. Rollups store t-digest sketches instead of pre-computed percentiles, letting later aggregation stay mathematically sound at the cost of roughly 3x more storage per rollup point than a plain scalar would need. We measured error against ground truth: t-digest-derived p99s stay within 2-4% of the true value even after two levels of re-aggregation (raw → 1min → 1hour).
slots.label: Downsampling rollups and how the planner picks a resolution

slots.sample: Rollups build progressively: raw → 1min (6hr delay) → 1hour (1 day delay) → 1day (1 week delay).
slots.label: Downsampling rollups and how the planner picks a resolution

slots.sample: The planner auto-selects resolution to match roughly 2-4 raw points per rendered pixel.
slots.label: Downsampling rollups and how the planner picks a resolution

slots.sample: Quantiles are rolled up as t-digest sketches, not scalars, keeping re-aggregated p99 within 2-4% of ground truth.
slots.label: Downsampling rollups and how the planner picks a resolution

slots.sample: Downsampling rollups and how the planner picks a resolution

slots.sample: A mobile client buffering telemetry offline for six hours will eventually flush it all at once. Helix's watermarking decides how long to wait before calling a window closed.
slots.label: Watermarks and late-arriving data in the ingest pipeline

slots.sample: Not every point arrives close to its own timestamp. Retry queues, offline-first mobile SDKs, and batched exporters can deliver data minutes or hours after it was generated. A rollup or sampling decision that closes its window too early silently drops that data; one that never closes never finishes computing.
slots.label: Watermarks and late-arriving data in the ingest pipeline

slots.sample: How the watermark advances
slots.label: Watermarks and late-arriving data in the ingest pipeline

slots.sample: Each ingestion shard tracks a watermark — the timestamp before which we're willing to say "no more data is coming." It advances based on the observed lateness distribution of recent traffic, not a fixed clock offset: if the shard has seen 99.5% of points for a given minute arrive within 45 seconds historically, the watermark trails real time by roughly that margin, recalculated every few minutes.
slots.label: Watermarks and late-arriving data in the ingest pipeline

slots.sample: What happens to data that misses the watermark
slots.label: Watermarks and late-arriving data in the ingest pipeline

slots.sample: Points arriving after the watermark has passed their timestamp aren't dropped — they're written to their correct time bucket in raw storage, but any rollup or tail-sampling decision already made for that window isn't retroactively recomputed by default. This is a deliberate tradeoff: recomputing closed rollups for late data would mean every downstream consumer (dashboards, alerts, exemplars) needs to handle values changing after the fact, which is worse for on-call trust than a rollup being very slightly under-counted.
slots.label: Watermarks and late-arriving data in the ingest pipeline

slots.sample: The opt-in correction path
slots.label: Watermarks and late-arriving data in the ingest pipeline

slots.sample: For workloads where correctness matters more than stability — billing-adjacent metrics, for instance — pipelines can enable `max_delay: 10m` with retroactive rollup correction, at the cost of holding rollup state open 10 minutes longer and a small compute overhead (roughly 4% more CPU on the compaction path) for periodic re-aggregation checks.
slots.label: Watermarks and late-arriving data in the ingest pipeline

slots.sample: What we've measured in practice
slots.label: Watermarks and late-arriving data in the ingest pipeline

slots.sample: Across our fleet, the default 99.5th-percentile watermark strategy captures 99.5% of points inside their correct window while adding a median 38-second delay before a 1-minute rollup is considered final — a delay dashboards absorb invisibly since they're rendering rollups a few minutes old anyway.
slots.label: Watermarks and late-arriving data in the ingest pipeline

slots.sample: Watermarks advance based on observed lateness percentiles, not a fixed offset.
slots.label: Watermarks and late-arriving data in the ingest pipeline

slots.sample: Late data past the watermark is stored correctly but doesn't retroactively reopen closed rollups by default.
slots.label: Watermarks and late-arriving data in the ingest pipeline

slots.sample: An opt-in correction mode exists for billing-sensitive pipelines, at roughly 4% extra compaction CPU.
slots.label: Watermarks and late-arriving data in the ingest pipeline

slots.sample: The fastest way to aggregate a billion rows is to never materialize them as rows. HelixQL pushes filters and partial aggregation down to the chunk scan itself.
slots.label: Pushdown: how summarize and where move into the storage layer

slots.sample: A naive query engine scans rows into memory, then filters, then aggregates — three separate passes over data that ballooned before it needed to. HelixQL pushes as much of that work as possible down into the chunk-scanning layer, so filtering and partial aggregation happen while data is still compressed.
slots.label: Pushdown: how summarize and where move into the storage layer

slots.sample: Filter pushdown against chunk metadata
slots.label: Pushdown: how summarize and where move into the storage layer

slots.sample: Every chunk carries a min/max summary for its value range and its label set reference. A `where value > 500` filter is checked against the chunk's max before a single point is decoded — if the chunk's max is 420, the whole chunk is skipped without decompression. On a representative query, this metadata-only skip eliminates 60-75% of candidate chunks before decode even starts.
slots.label: Pushdown: how summarize and where move into the storage layer

slots.sample: Partial aggregation during scan
slots.label: Pushdown: how summarize and where move into the storage layer

slots.sample: For `summarize sum()/count()/avg()`, the storage layer doesn't materialize every decoded point into a row buffer — it accumulates the aggregate directly as it decodes each chunk, discarding individual values immediately. This keeps memory flat regardless of how many points are scanned, instead of scaling with row count.
slots.label: Pushdown: how summarize and where move into the storage layer

slots.sample: In this query, both `where` clauses and the `summarize` push all the way down to the chunk scan — the query engine above storage never sees an individual data point, only partial per-chunk aggregates that get merged.
slots.label: Pushdown: how summarize and where move into the storage layer

slots.sample: What can't be pushed down
slots.label: Pushdown: how summarize and where move into the storage layer

slots.sample: Percentile aggregations (`p95`, `p99`) can't be fully pushed down the same way, since a true percentile needs the full distribution, not a partial sum. Instead, storage pushes down a t-digest sketch construction per chunk, which is still far cheaper than materializing raw rows — sketch construction costs about 3x a simple sum/count pass, versus the 15-40x cost of materializing full rows for percentile computation upstream.
slots.label: Pushdown: how summarize and where move into the storage layer

slots.sample: Measured impact
slots.label: Pushdown: how summarize and where move into the storage layer

slots.sample: On a benchmark query scanning 40,000 chunks with a selective filter, full pushdown (filter + partial aggregation) completes in 210ms and holds under 40MB of working memory. The same query with pushdown disabled — materializing filtered rows before aggregating — takes 2.8s and peaks at 1.1GB of memory.
slots.label: Pushdown: how summarize and where move into the storage layer

slots.sample: Chunk-level min/max metadata skips 60-75% of candidate chunks before any decompression.
slots.label: Pushdown: how summarize and where move into the storage layer

slots.sample: Partial aggregation during scan keeps memory flat instead of scaling with matched row count.
slots.label: Pushdown: how summarize and where move into the storage layer

slots.sample: Percentile aggregations push down as t-digest sketch construction, not full pushdown, but still avoid row materialization.
slots.label: Pushdown: how summarize and where move into the storage layer

slots.sample: Finding one trace_id among billions of spans shouldn't require touching every segment. A per-segment bloom filter turns most lookups into a negative in microseconds.
slots.label: A bloom filter index for trace_id lookups at 40M spans/day

slots.sample: A single-trace lookup — "show me trace a93f7c2e..." — is the most common query shape in Helix's tracing UI, and also the easiest to get catastrophically wrong at scale. With 40 million spans a day and 90 days of retention, that's up to 3.6 billion spans a lookup could theoretically touch.
slots.label: A bloom filter index for trace_id lookups at 40M spans/day

slots.sample: Why a global index doesn't work here
slots.label: A bloom filter index for trace_id lookups at 40M spans/day

slots.sample: A single global trace_id index sounds appealing, but trace_ids are effectively random UUIDs — there's no locality to exploit, and a B-tree or hash index over billions of entries, kept mutable as new segments arrive and old ones expire, becomes a write-amplification and compaction headache of its own.
slots.label: A bloom filter index for trace_id lookups at 40M spans/day

slots.sample: The bloom filter approach
slots.label: A bloom filter index for trace_id lookups at 40M spans/day

slots.sample: Instead, every immutable trace segment (roughly 15 minutes of spans, around 45,000 spans per segment at our reference load) gets a bloom filter built once at segment-close time, sized for a 0.1% false-positive rate at expected cardinality. Looking up a trace_id means checking the bloom filter for every segment in the retention window first — a check that costs about 180 nanoseconds per segment.
slots.label: A bloom filter index for trace_id lookups at 40M spans/day

slots.sample: The math that makes this work
slots.label: A bloom filter index for trace_id lookups at 40M spans/day

slots.sample: Checking 8,640 bloom filters at 180ns each costs about 1.6ms total — negligible. At a 0.1% false-positive rate, roughly 8-9 of those 8,640 segments will falsely report a possible match and need to be opened and checked directly, each costing around 4ms to scan its trace_id dictionary. Total worst-case cost for a 90-day trace lookup: roughly 1.6ms of bloom checks plus 35-40ms of false-positive verification — well under 50ms for a query that could otherwise mean opening thousands of segment files.
slots.label: A bloom filter index for trace_id lookups at 40M spans/day

slots.sample: Sizing the false-positive rate
slots.label: A bloom filter index for trace_id lookups at 40M spans/day

slots.sample: We tuned the 0.1% target by trading bloom filter memory against false-positive verification cost: a looser 1% rate shrinks filter memory by roughly 40% but multiplies false-positive segment opens tenfold, pushing worst-case lookup latency past 200ms. At our current 0.1% setting, bloom filters across a 90-day retention window for a mid-size tenant cost about 340MB of memory total — cheap compared to the alternative.
slots.label: A bloom filter index for trace_id lookups at 40M spans/day

slots.sample: Every 15-minute trace segment gets an immutable bloom filter at close time, tuned to 0.1% false-positive rate.
slots.label: A bloom filter index for trace_id lookups at 40M spans/day

slots.sample: A 90-day trace_id lookup costs roughly 1.6ms of bloom checks plus 35-40ms of false-positive verification.
slots.label: A bloom filter index for trace_id lookups at 40M spans/day

slots.sample: Fresh ingest produces lots of small, loosely-packed segments. Compaction merges them into fewer, denser ones — but has to do it without blocking reads.
slots.label: Segment compaction: merging small chunks without stalling queries

slots.sample: Data lands from ingestion in small, frequently-flushed segments — good for low write latency, bad for long-term query efficiency, since scanning 200 small segments costs more open/seek overhead than scanning 10 well-packed ones covering the same data. Compaction exists to close that gap, continuously, in the background.
slots.label: Segment compaction: merging small chunks without stalling queries

slots.sample: The compaction tiers
slots.label: Segment compaction: merging small chunks without stalling queries

slots.sample: Helix runs three compaction tiers: L0 merges raw 15-minute segments into 2-hour segments within the first few hours after ingest; L1 merges those into 1-day segments after 24 hours; L2 merges a week of L1 segments into a single monthly segment once data has aged past the point where late arrivals are expected. Each tier roughly halves segment count while improving average chunk density.
slots.label: Segment compaction: merging small chunks without stalling queries

slots.sample: Staying out of the query path
slots.label: Segment compaction: merging small chunks without stalling queries

slots.sample: Compaction reads source segments and writes a new merged segment without touching the originals until the merge is verified complete, then atomically swaps a segment-manifest pointer. Queries in flight against the old segments finish against them; new queries pick up the compacted version — there's no lock, no stall, just a brief window where both versions exist on disk.
slots.label: Segment compaction: merging small chunks without stalling queries

slots.sample: The cost of falling behind
slots.label: Segment compaction: merging small chunks without stalling queries

slots.sample: If compaction falls behind — usually from a sudden ingest spike or a compaction-worker outage — queries against the affected window degrade gracefully but measurably: we've seen a query touching an under-compacted 24-hour window take 3-4x longer than the same query against a fully compacted equivalent, purely from segment-open overhead. This is why `io_priority: below_normal` still gets a floor: compaction can be deprioritized during load spikes but never starved indefinitely.
slots.label: Segment compaction: merging small chunks without stalling queries

slots.sample: What we measured in steady state
slots.label: Segment compaction: merging small chunks without stalling queries

slots.sample: Across our fleet, L0 compaction typically completes within 15 minutes of its trigger, keeping the "hot" window (data under 3 hours old) at roughly 4-6 segments per shard instead of the 12+ it would otherwise accumulate. That density difference is worth about a 2.3x improvement in query latency for dashboards refreshing on recent data, which is most of them.
slots.label: Segment compaction: merging small chunks without stalling queries

slots.sample: Three compaction tiers progressively merge 15-min segments into 2-hour, then daily, then monthly segments.
slots.label: Segment compaction: merging small chunks without stalling queries

slots.sample: Compaction never locks readers — it swaps a manifest pointer atomically after a verified merge.
slots.label: Segment compaction: merging small chunks without stalling queries

slots.sample: Falling behind on compaction costs 3-4x query latency on affected windows from segment-open overhead alone.

slots.sample: Every point needs to survive a crash before it's acknowledged. Group commit is what keeps that durability guarantee from tanking throughput.
slots.label: The write-ahead log: durability without doubling ingest latency

slots.sample: Acknowledging a write before it's durable is a data-loss bug waiting for a bad day. Fsyncing on every individual point is durable but slow — a single fsync on our reference NVMe hardware costs around 0.4-0.8ms, which would cap single-threaded ingest at roughly 1,500 points/sec if done per point. Helix's WAL uses group commit to get both.
slots.label: The write-ahead log: durability without doubling ingest latency

slots.sample: How group commit works
slots.label: The write-ahead log: durability without doubling ingest latency

slots.sample: Writes from many concurrent ingest connections accumulate into a shared per-shard buffer. A dedicated WAL writer thread flushes and fsyncs that buffer on whichever comes first: a 10ms timer or a 4MB buffer fill. Every writer waiting on that fsync gets acknowledged together, in one syscall, regardless of how many individual writes were batched.
slots.label: The write-ahead log: durability without doubling ingest latency

slots.sample: What this buys in practice
slots.label: The write-ahead log: durability without doubling ingest latency

slots.sample: On a shard receiving 12,000 points/sec across 200 concurrent connections, group commit means roughly one fsync every 10ms instead of 12,000 — a 99.2% reduction in fsync calls, at the cost of adding up to 10ms of latency to the slowest write in each batch. Measured p50 durability latency including WAL fsync: 6.8ms. p99: 14.2ms, mostly batches that landed right at the buffer-fill boundary.
slots.label: The write-ahead log: durability without doubling ingest latency

slots.sample: Why the WAL is per-shard, not global
slots.label: The write-ahead log: durability without doubling ingest latency

slots.sample: A single global WAL would serialize every write in the cluster through one fsync stream, an obvious bottleneck. Per-shard WALs let fsync throughput scale roughly linearly with shard count, since each shard's writer thread and disk queue are independent. The tradeoff is that a crash recovery has to replay N independent WALs instead of one, but that only matters at restart, not on the hot path.
slots.label: The write-ahead log: durability without doubling ingest latency

slots.sample: Recovery cost
slots.label: The write-ahead log: durability without doubling ingest latency

slots.sample: On restart after an unclean shutdown, WAL replay for a shard with a typical 4MB of unflushed-to-chunk-storage data takes under 400ms — we cap unreplayed WAL size specifically to keep recovery time bounded, since a shard that can't come back online within a second or two starts affecting cluster-wide availability during a rolling restart.

slots.sample: Shard by trace_id and a single trace lives on one node, but a service-wide query fans out everywhere. Shard by service and it's the reverse. Helix does neither purely.
slots.label: Sharding traces by trace_id vs by service: a storage tradeoff

slots.sample: Every distributed trace store faces this choice at the storage layer: shard spans by trace_id, so an entire trace always lives together, or shard by service, so a query for "all checkout-api spans" hits one place. Each choice makes the other query pattern expensive. Helix uses a hybrid.
slots.label: Sharding traces by trace_id vs by service: a storage tradeoff

slots.sample: The pure trace_id-sharding cost
slots.label: Sharding traces by trace_id vs by service: a storage tradeoff

slots.sample: Sharding purely by trace_id (hash of trace_id mod shard count) makes single-trace lookups perfect — one shard, one lookup. But it scatters a service's spans uniformly across every shard, so a query like "p99 duration for checkout-api over the last hour" has to fan out to all N shards even though it never needs to reconstruct a full trace. On a 64-shard cluster, that's 64x the query fan-out for a query pattern that's arguably more common than single-trace lookups.
slots.label: Sharding traces by trace_id vs by service: a storage tradeoff

slots.sample: The pure service-sharding cost
slots.label: Sharding traces by trace_id vs by service: a storage tradeoff

slots.sample: The reverse holds too: shard by service, and service-wide aggregation is fast and local, but a single trace spans multiple services by definition — a checkout request touches checkout-api, payments-api, and inventory-api spans, which now live on three different shards, meaning single-trace reconstruction always fans out.
slots.label: Sharding traces by trace_id vs by service: a storage tradeoff

slots.sample: Helix's hybrid: shard by service, index by trace_id
slots.label: Sharding traces by trace_id vs by service: a storage tradeoff

slots.sample: We primarily shard by service, since service-scoped aggregation is the dominant query pattern in dashboards and alerting — roughly 78% of production trace queries in our telemetry are service-scoped, not trace-scoped. Single-trace lookups fan out across the (typically small, 3-6 service) set of shards involved, located via the bloom-filter segment index described elsewhere, rather than scattering to all shards.
slots.label: Sharding traces by trace_id vs by service: a storage tradeoff

slots.sample: Measured cost of the hybrid
slots.label: Sharding traces by trace_id vs by service: a storage tradeoff

slots.sample: Service-scoped aggregation queries average 90ms on a 64-shard cluster, versus an estimated 310ms if trace_id sharding forced full fan-out for the same query. Single-trace lookups average 140ms under service sharding — slower than the theoretical best case of pure trace_id sharding (roughly 40ms) but that's a cost we accept for the majority query pattern winning by 3.4x.
slots.label: Sharding traces by trace_id vs by service: a storage tradeoff

slots.sample: Processing one row at a time means a branch and a function call per value. Vectorized execution processes thousands at once, and the CPU notices.
slots.label: Vectorized execution: batching HelixQL operators over column batches

slots.sample: A naive query engine evaluates each operator row by row: check a filter, branch, maybe emit. That pattern defeats CPU pipelining and wastes cache bandwidth on function-call overhead. HelixQL's execution engine instead operates on batches of a few thousand values at a time, column by column.
slots.label: Vectorized execution: batching HelixQL operators over column batches

slots.sample: What a batch looks like
slots.label: Vectorized execution: batching HelixQL operators over column batches

slots.sample: Decoded chunk data is materialized into fixed-size batches — 2,048 values per batch, chosen to fit comfortably in L2 cache alongside the operator's working state. A `where value > 500` filter, instead of branching per row, produces a selection bitmap over the whole batch in one tight loop with no branch misprediction on the comparison itself.
slots.label: Vectorized execution: batching HelixQL operators over column batches

slots.sample: Measured CPU impact
slots.label: Vectorized execution: batching HelixQL operators over column batches

slots.sample: On a benchmark scanning 100 million points with two numeric filters and a group-by aggregation, vectorized batch execution completed in 1.4s using a single core. The same query plan executed row-at-a-time (a mode we kept for correctness testing and debugging) took 6.1s — a 4.4x difference attributable almost entirely to eliminated branch mispredictions and better instruction cache locality.
slots.label: Vectorized execution: batching HelixQL operators over column batches

slots.sample: Where vectorization breaks down
slots.label: Vectorized execution: batching HelixQL operators over column batches

slots.sample: Not every operator vectorizes cleanly. Regex-based log filtering, for instance, still evaluates largely per-value since general regex engines don't have a natural batched form — we get some benefit from batching the memory access pattern, but the regex evaluation itself remains the bottleneck, typically 8-10x slower per byte than a numeric comparison at the same batch size.
slots.label: Vectorized execution: batching HelixQL operators over column batches

slots.sample: Why 2,048 and not larger
slots.label: Vectorized execution: batching HelixQL operators over column batches

slots.sample: We tested batch sizes from 256 to 16,384. Beyond 2,048, batches started spilling out of L2 cache on our reference hardware (256KB L2 per core), and the marginal throughput gain from fewer batch-boundary overheads was outweighed by cache misses — we measured a 12% throughput regression at 8,192 versus 2,048 for typical filter-heavy queries.
slots.label: Vectorized execution: batching HelixQL operators over column batches

slots.sample: Query execution operates on 2,048-value column batches, not individual rows.
slots.label: Vectorized execution: batching HelixQL operators over column batches

slots.sample: Vectorized filter/aggregation is roughly 4.4x faster than row-at-a-time execution on numeric workloads.
slots.label: Vectorized execution: batching HelixQL operators over column batches

slots.sample: Regex-based log filters don't vectorize cleanly and remain the slower operator class.
slots.label: Vectorized execution: batching HelixQL operators over column batches

slots.sample: Vectorized execution: batching HelixQL operators over column batches

slots.sample: Not all data needs to sit on NVMe. Helix moves aging segments through storage tiers automatically, and the planner has to know which tier it's scanning.
slots.label: Retention tiers: hot SSD, warm object storage, and the tier-aware scan

slots.sample: Keeping 13 months of full-resolution data on NVMe would be economically absurd for most workloads. Helix ages data through three storage tiers — hot local SSD, warm object storage with a local cache, and cold object storage — and the query planner has to account for wildly different access latencies across them.
slots.label: Retention tiers: hot SSD, warm object storage, and the tier-aware scan

slots.sample: The tiers, by age
slots.label: Retention tiers: hot SSD, warm object storage, and the tier-aware scan

slots.sample: Data under 3 hours old lives on local NVMe (hot). From 3 hours to 7 days, it moves to object storage but stays in a local read-through cache seeded on access (warm). Past 7 days, it's object storage only, uncached until requested (cold). Movement between tiers happens as part of the compaction passes described elsewhere, so tiering and compaction share a background worker pool rather than running as separate jobs.
slots.label: Retention tiers: hot SSD, warm object storage, and the tier-aware scan

slots.sample: Why the planner needs to know the tier
slots.label: Retention tiers: hot SSD, warm object storage, and the tier-aware scan

slots.sample: A chunk fetch from hot NVMe averages 80 microseconds. The same fetch from warm cache, on a cache hit, averages 400 microseconds; on a cache miss, it's an object storage round trip averaging 12-18ms. Cold tier fetches are always that 12-18ms round trip. If the planner assumed uniform latency, it would badly underestimate query cost for anything touching data older than a week, and could choose a join or scan order that makes sense for NVMe but is disastrous for a fan-out of object storage requests.
slots.label: Retention tiers: hot SSD, warm object storage, and the tier-aware scan

slots.sample: Batching cold-tier fetches
slots.label: Retention tiers: hot SSD, warm object storage, and the tier-aware scan

slots.sample: To avoid paying that 12-18ms round trip per chunk, cold-tier scans batch fetch requests — up to 64 chunks per object storage GET where the storage layout allows it — instead of issuing one request per chunk. This turns what would be an 18-second scan (1,000 chunks × 18ms sequential) into roughly 280ms of batched, parallelized fetches on the same query.
slots.label: Retention tiers: hot SSD, warm object storage, and the tier-aware scan

slots.sample: What this costs customers
slots.label: Retention tiers: hot SSD, warm object storage, and the tier-aware scan

slots.sample: In our published cost model, a query touching only hot-tier data costs roughly 1/150th what an equivalent cold-tier query costs in compute-seconds, which is why dashboards defaulting to a 24-hour view stay cheap by construction, and why we surface tier information in query plan output so teams can see when a "simple" historical query is quietly expensive.
slots.label: Retention tiers: hot SSD, warm object storage, and the tier-aware scan

slots.sample: Three tiers age data by time: hot NVMe (0-3h), warm cached object storage (3h-7d), cold object storage (7d+).
slots.label: Retention tiers: hot SSD, warm object storage, and the tier-aware scan

slots.sample: Cold-tier chunk fetches cost 12-18ms each; the planner batches up to 64 per request to avoid serial round trips.
slots.label: Retention tiers: hot SSD, warm object storage, and the tier-aware scan

slots.sample: Hot-tier queries cost roughly 1/150th of equivalent cold-tier queries in compute-seconds.
slots.label: Retention tiers: hot SSD, warm object storage, and the tier-aware scan

slots.sample: A HelixQL query with four correlated signals has 24 possible join orders. The planner doesn't try them all — here's the search it actually runs.
slots.label: Building the query planner's join order search

slots.sample: Join order matters enormously for multi-way correlation queries — joining metrics, traces, logs, and profiles in the wrong order can mean materializing an intermediate result 100x larger than necessary. With n relations there are n! possible orders, which gets expensive to search exhaustively past 4-5 inputs. HelixQL's planner uses a bounded dynamic-programming search instead.
slots.label: Building the query planner's join order search

slots.sample: Why exhaustive search doesn't scale
slots.label: Building the query planner's join order search

slots.sample: Most HelixQL queries join 2-3 signal types, where exhaustive search (6 or 24 orderings) is trivially cheap — under a millisecond of planning time. But queries correlating 5+ sources, which do happen in complex incident investigations, would require searching 120+ orderings if done naively, each requiring a cost estimate.
slots.label: Building the query planner's join order search

slots.sample: The DP approach
slots.label: Building the query planner's join order search

slots.sample: The planner builds up optimal join orders for subsets of relations incrementally: it finds the best plan for every pair, then extends each to the best plan for every triple that includes an already-optimal pair, and so on. This bounds the search to roughly 2^n subsets rather than n! full orderings — for 5 relations, that's 32 subset evaluations instead of 120 full permutations.
slots.label: Building the query planner's join order search

slots.sample: Pruning beyond DP
slots.label: Building the query planner's join order search

slots.sample: Even 2^n subset evaluation gets expensive past 7-8 relations, which is rare but not impossible in exploratory investigation queries. Past that threshold, the planner switches to a greedy heuristic — always join the two smallest estimated intermediate results next — which sacrifices optimality for bounded planning time. We cap planning time itself at 50ms; if DP search would exceed that budget, it falls back to greedy before that budget is spent.
slots.label: Building the query planner's join order search

slots.sample: Measured plan quality
slots.label: Building the query planner's join order search

slots.sample: Against a benchmark of 30 real-world multi-signal correlation queries pulled from customer incident investigations, the DP-based planner found the truly optimal join order in 27 of 30 cases (the other 3 were close, within 15% of optimal cost), and did so in under 8ms of planning time for the median query, versus roughly 40ms if we forced exhaustive search on every query regardless of size.
slots.label: Building the query planner's join order search

slots.sample: DP-based join order search bounds planning to roughly 2^n subsets instead of n! full permutations.
slots.label: Building the query planner's join order search

slots.sample: Planning time is capped at 50ms; past that, the planner falls back to a greedy smallest-first heuristic.
slots.label: Building the query planner's join order search

slots.sample: A flaky network link between a collector and Helix causes retries. Retries cause duplicate spans. Here's how the ingest path keeps duplicates from doubling your trace counts.
slots.label: Span deduplication when OTel collectors retry

slots.sample: OTLP exporters retry on ambiguous failures — a timeout doesn't tell you whether the server received and processed the batch or not. Retrying is the correct, safe default, but it means Helix's ingest path has to assume duplicate spans arrive regularly, not as a rare edge case.
slots.label: Span deduplication when OTel collectors retry

slots.sample: How often this actually happens
slots.label: Span deduplication when OTel collectors retry

slots.sample: Across our fleet, we measure retry-induced duplicate spans at roughly 0.3% of total span volume in steady state, spiking to 2-3% during network-degraded periods or collector restarts. At 40 million spans/day for a mid-size tenant, even the steady-state rate is 120,000 potential duplicate spans daily — enough to visibly skew count-based metrics if left unhandled.
slots.label: Span deduplication when OTel collectors retry

slots.sample: The dedup key
slots.label: Span deduplication when OTel collectors retry

slots.sample: Each span carries a deterministic identity: trace_id + span_id, which OTel guarantees is stable across retries of the same span (the exporter doesn't regenerate IDs on retry, it resends the same object). Ingest checks incoming span_ids against a per-shard bloom filter of recently-seen span_ids — a rolling 10-minute window, since duplicates from retries arrive within seconds to low minutes of the original in practice.
slots.label: Span deduplication when OTel collectors retry

slots.sample: Why a bloom filter and not an exact set
slots.label: Span deduplication when OTel collectors retry

slots.sample: An exact deduplication set for 10 minutes of span_ids at fleet scale would mean tracking potentially hundreds of millions of UUIDs in memory. The bloom filter, tuned to a 0.5% false-positive rate at this scale, costs a fraction of that memory — roughly 180MB per shard for our reference throughput — at the cost of very rarely dropping a legitimately unique span that happens to collide. We accept that tradeoff because a rare dropped unique span is less harmful than either unbounded memory growth or letting real duplicates through.
slots.label: Span deduplication when OTel collectors retry

slots.sample: What this means for counts
slots.label: Span deduplication when OTel collectors retry

slots.sample: Before dedup shipped, we saw customer-reported anomalies where `count()` aggregations over spans during a known network-flaky period ran 2-4% high compared to expected traffic — entirely attributable to retry duplicates. Post-dedup, that discrepancy dropped to under 0.1% in the same conditions.
slots.label: Span deduplication when OTel collectors retry

slots.sample: Retry-induced duplicate spans run about 0.3% of volume in steady state, up to 2-3% during network degradation.
slots.label: Span deduplication when OTel collectors retry

slots.sample: Dedup uses a rolling 10-minute bloom filter keyed on trace_id + span_id, costing ~180MB per shard.
slots.label: Span deduplication when OTel collectors retry

slots.sample: Post-dedup, count anomalies during flaky-network periods dropped from 2-4% to under 0.1%.

slots.sample: With thousands of spans closing every second, most exemplar candidates have to be rejected. The selection algorithm decides which ones are actually useful later.
slots.label: The exemplar sampler: choosing which points earn a trace link

slots.sample: Attaching a trace_id to a histogram bucket is cheap per-event, but deciding which of thousands of candidate spans deserves that slot is where the real design work is. A naive "first one wins" or "random sample" strategy tends to attach boring, unhelpful exemplars — a request that happened to close first, not one that tells you anything.
slots.label: The exemplar sampler: choosing which points earn a trace link

slots.sample: The scoring function
slots.label: The exemplar sampler: choosing which points earn a trace link

slots.sample: Each candidate span is scored on a combination of factors: how extreme its duration is relative to the bucket's recent distribution, whether its status is an error, and whether it's already the exemplar for a different, less-populated bucket (to avoid over-concentrating exemplars on one unusually chatty request). The highest-scoring candidate per bucket per 15-second window wins the slot.
slots.label: The exemplar sampler: choosing which points earn a trace link

slots.sample: Why we don't always replace on a better score
slots.label: The exemplar sampler: choosing which points earn a trace link

slots.sample: Early versions replaced the exemplar on any strictly higher score, which caused a problem: exemplars would churn every few seconds as marginally-more-extreme spans arrived, making a dashboard panel's "view trace" link point somewhere different every time someone refreshed. We added a replacement threshold — a new candidate must score at least 0.15 higher (on a normalized 0-1 scale) to displace the current exemplar — which cut exemplar churn by roughly 70% while keeping genuinely more useful traces winning out.
slots.label: The exemplar sampler: choosing which points earn a trace link

slots.sample: Error-status weighting
slots.label: The exemplar sampler: choosing which points earn a trace link

slots.sample: Error spans get a strong scoring boost (weight 0.4 of the total) because an on-call engineer investigating a spike almost always wants an error example over a merely-slow one, even in a latency-focused histogram. We validated this weighting against actual incident retro data: in the 90 days before this weighting shipped, engineers manually searched for an error trace instead of using the attached exemplar in about 40% of latency-related incidents; after, that dropped to roughly 11%.
slots.label: The exemplar sampler: choosing which points earn a trace link

slots.sample: What this means for dashboard trust
slots.label: The exemplar sampler: choosing which points earn a trace link

slots.sample: The practical outcome is that clicking an exemplar link on a spike almost always lands on a trace that's actually representative of what went wrong, not an arbitrary one — which is the entire value proposition of exemplars in the first place. We keep tuning the weights quarterly against fresh incident retro data rather than treating the scoring function as fixed, since traffic patterns and error signatures shift enough across two or three quarters that a weighting tuned for one season of traffic can quietly go stale for the next.
slots.label: The exemplar sampler: choosing which points earn a trace link

slots.sample: Two different metrics on the same pod share most of their label set. A per-metric dictionary wastes that overlap; a shared vocabulary captures it.
slots.label: Compressing high-cardinality label dictionaries with a shared vocabulary

slots.sample: Dictionary encoding already cuts label-set storage substantially, as covered elsewhere, but a naive per-metric dictionary still misses an obvious win: `service=checkout-api, pod=checkout-7f9d` appears identically across a dozen different metric names on the same pod. A shared, cross-metric vocabulary captures that overlap.
slots.label: Compressing high-cardinality label dictionaries with a shared vocabulary

slots.sample: Splitting label sets into components
slots.label: Compressing high-cardinality label dictionaries with a shared vocabulary

slots.sample: Instead of dictionary-encoding a full label set as one opaque string, Helix decomposes it into individual key=value tokens, and interns each token independently into a shard-wide token dictionary. A label set then becomes a short array of token IDs rather than one string ID, letting `service=checkout-api` share a single dictionary entry across every metric and every pod that carries it.
slots.label: Compressing high-cardinality label dictionaries with a shared vocabulary

slots.sample: Where the extra win comes from
slots.label: Compressing high-cardinality label dictionaries with a shared vocabulary

slots.sample: The whole-set dictionary from our earlier design already got label sets down to 4 bytes per reference, which sounds like it beats the 12-byte token-array approach on paper. The real win is elsewhere: with a whole-set dictionary, `region=us-east-1` existing inside 50 different metrics' worth of label sets meant 50 different whole-set dictionary entries, each storing that substring redundantly. Token-level sharing collapses that redundancy at the dictionary level itself, not just at the reference level.
slots.label: Compressing high-cardinality label dictionaries with a shared vocabulary

slots.sample: Measured impact
slots.label: Compressing high-cardinality label dictionaries with a shared vocabulary

slots.sample: On a representative shard carrying 180 distinct metric names across 12,000 pods, the whole-set dictionary held about 940,000 entries with significant internal string redundancy, totaling roughly 61MB compressed. The token-vocabulary redesign reduced the underlying dictionary to about 38,000 unique tokens (service names, pod names, region values, etc.) at just 4.1MB compressed — a 93% reduction in dictionary size, even though individual label-set references grew slightly.
slots.label: Compressing high-cardinality label dictionaries with a shared vocabulary

slots.sample: The lookup cost tradeoff
slots.label: Compressing high-cardinality label dictionaries with a shared vocabulary

slots.sample: Resolving a full label set now means N token lookups instead of one whole-set lookup, where N is typically 4-8 for a realistic label set. Measured average resolution cost went from about 40ns (single lookup) to roughly 140ns (multiple token lookups) — a real but small cost, easily absorbed given how rarely label sets need full string resolution versus being compared as token-ID arrays directly.
slots.label: Compressing high-cardinality label dictionaries with a shared vocabulary

slots.sample: Label sets are decomposed into individual key=value tokens, shared across all metrics on a shard.
slots.label: Compressing high-cardinality label dictionaries with a shared vocabulary

slots.sample: Measured dictionary size reduction: 93% (61MB to 4.1MB) on a representative 12,000-pod shard.
slots.label: Compressing high-cardinality label dictionaries with a shared vocabulary

slots.sample: Full label-set resolution cost rose from ~40ns to ~140ns, a worthwhile tradeoff given the storage win.

slots.sample: A 'summarize ... by' clause looks simple in HelixQL syntax, but resolving it against dynamic labels, computed expressions, and bucketed time takes real planning work.
slots.label: How HelixQL resolves by clauses into group keys

slots.sample: The `by` clause in a HelixQL `summarize` looks like straightforward SQL `GROUP BY`, but HelixQL's label model — where every series can carry a different set of labels — means group-key resolution has to handle missing labels, computed grouping expressions, and time bucketing all in the same pass.
slots.label: How HelixQL resolves by clauses into group keys

slots.sample: Static label grouping
slots.label: How HelixQL resolves by clauses into group keys

slots.sample: The simple case, grouping by a label that's present on every matched series, resolves directly against the token-vocabulary label sets described elsewhere — the group key is just the token ID (or IDs, for multi-label grouping) for that label's value, no string comparison needed at execution time.
slots.label: How HelixQL resolves by clauses into group keys

slots.sample: The missing-label case
slots.label: How HelixQL resolves by clauses into group keys

slots.sample: Not every series carries every label — grouping by `pod` when 2% of matched series come from a job that doesn't set a pod label at all needs a defined behavior, not a crash. HelixQL treats a missing grouping label as an explicit `null` group, aggregated separately and clearly labeled in results rather than silently dropped or merged into an arbitrary bucket.
slots.label: How HelixQL resolves by clauses into group keys

slots.sample: Computed grouping expressions
slots.label: How HelixQL resolves by clauses into group keys

slots.sample: Grouping by an expression — `by bin(timestamp, 5m)`, or `by strcat(service, '/', env)` — can't use the pre-built token dictionary directly, since the group key doesn't exist until the expression is evaluated. These paths fall back to computing the expression per row (or per batch, under vectorized execution) and hashing the result into a group key on the fly, which costs measurably more than static label grouping — about 3-5x, from our benchmarks — but is still cheap relative to the aggregation itself for typical cardinalities.
slots.label: How HelixQL resolves by clauses into group keys

slots.sample: Group key cardinality limits
slots.label: How HelixQL resolves by clauses into group keys

slots.sample: A `summarize ... by` clause grouping on a high-cardinality field (accidentally grouping by `trace_id` instead of `route`, for instance) can produce an enormous result set. The planner estimates result cardinality using the same histogram statistics that drive filter selectivity, and rejects queries whose estimated group count exceeds a configurable ceiling (default 500,000 groups) before execution even starts, rather than letting a query silently consume unbounded memory building group state.
slots.label: How HelixQL resolves by clauses into group keys

slots.sample: Static label grouping resolves directly against pre-built token IDs; missing labels group into an explicit null bucket.
slots.label: How HelixQL resolves by clauses into group keys

slots.sample: Computed grouping expressions (bin(), string concatenation) cost 3-5x more than static label grouping.
slots.label: How HelixQL resolves by clauses into group keys

slots.sample: The planner rejects queries whose estimated group cardinality exceeds 500,000 before execution starts.
slots.label: How HelixQL resolves by clauses into group keys

slots.sample: A sustained ingest spike can outpace background compaction. Helix has to decide who slows down first, and it's a deliberately ordered list.
slots.label: Backpressure: what happens when ingestion outruns compaction

slots.sample: Under normal load, ingestion and compaction run at a comfortable pace relative to each other. Under a sustained spike — a customer's traffic doubling, or a large batch backfill — ingestion can outpace compaction's ability to keep segment counts under control. Something has to give, and Helix has a defined order for what gives first.
slots.label: Backpressure: what happens when ingestion outruns compaction

slots.sample: The signal that triggers backpressure
slots.label: Backpressure: what happens when ingestion outruns compaction

slots.sample: Each shard tracks its uncompacted segment count as the primary backpressure signal, rather than raw ingest rate, since segment count is what actually determines query cost degradation described elsewhere. Crossing a first threshold (default 20 uncompacted L0 segments) triggers the first response tier; a second threshold (40 segments) triggers a harder one.
slots.label: Backpressure: what happens when ingestion outruns compaction

slots.sample: Tier 1: reprioritize, don't reject
slots.label: Backpressure: what happens when ingestion outruns compaction

slots.sample: Tier 2 and 3: shedding and pushback
slots.label: Backpressure: what happens when ingestion outruns compaction

slots.sample: If boosting compaction priority alone doesn't stop segment count from climbing — typically because the spike is simply too large for available compaction throughput — tier 2 sheds the lowest-value writes first: debug-level logs and already-sampled-down metrics, which customers configure as explicitly droppable under load. Tier 3, reached only in sustained severe spikes (we've hit it a handful of times fleet-wide in the past year), applies real ingest backpressure: 429 responses with a retry-after header, pushing the problem back to client-side buffering rather than letting the shard fall further behind.
slots.label: Backpressure: what happens when ingestion outruns compaction

slots.sample: Why segment count and not queue depth
slots.label: Backpressure: what happens when ingestion outruns compaction

slots.sample: We considered using WAL queue depth as the backpressure signal instead, since it's more directly tied to write latency. We rejected it because queue depth is noisy on short timescales and reacts to momentary bursts that resolve themselves within seconds. Segment count is a slower-moving, more stable signal that better reflects genuine sustained pressure rather than normal traffic jitter — we measured roughly 4x fewer false-positive backpressure triggers using segment count over a 30-day comparison window. In the 14 months this system has been live, tier 1 activates a few times a week fleet-wide, invisible to customers beyond a brief compaction priority bump. Tier 2 activates roughly monthly, usually during a large customer's traffic event, and is visible only if a team explicitly opted debug logs into the droppable category. Tier 3 has fired 3 times, always during a genuine multi-minute traffic anomaly, and resolved within 90 seconds of the spike subsiding each time.
slots.label: Backpressure: what happens when ingestion outruns compaction

slots.sample: Backpressure escalates in three tiers, gated on uncompacted segment count, not raw ingest rate or queue depth.
slots.label: Backpressure: what happens when ingestion outruns compaction

slots.sample: Tier 1 reprioritizes compaction; tier 2 sheds low-value writes; tier 3 applies real 429 backpressure to clients.
slots.label: Backpressure: what happens when ingestion outruns compaction

slots.sample: Continuous profiling produces a full stack sample every 10ms per core. Storing each one independently would be absurd — Helix stores deltas against a shared call-tree instead.
slots.label: Profiling data as a fourth signal: storing stack traces as flame-graph deltas

slots.sample: Continuous profiling adds a fourth signal alongside metrics, logs, and traces: periodic stack samples, typically every 10ms per core under CPU profiling. At that rate, a single 16-core host produces 1,600 stack samples a second. Storing each as an independent list of frames would be enormous and mostly redundant, since most samples share the bulk of their call tree with the sample before them.
slots.label: Profiling data as a fourth signal: storing stack traces as flame-graph deltas

slots.sample: The shared call-tree structure
slots.label: Profiling data as a fourth signal: storing stack traces as flame-graph deltas

slots.sample: Instead of storing each sample as a flat frame list, Helix maintains a shared call-tree per profiled process, where each unique function-call path is a node visited once, and a sample is stored as a reference to the deepest node it reached plus a hit-count increment along that path. Two samples that share the same call path up to frame 12 and diverge after that only cost storage for the divergent tail.
slots.label: Profiling data as a fourth signal: storing stack traces as flame-graph deltas

slots.sample: Measured storage impact
slots.label: Profiling data as a fourth signal: storing stack traces as flame-graph deltas

slots.sample: On a representative profiling session — 16 cores, 10ms sampling, one hour, roughly 5.76 million individual stack samples — a naive flat-frame-list encoding would cost approximately 890MB uncompressed (averaging ~155 bytes per sample across typical stack depths of 20-40 frames). The shared call-tree delta encoding brought that down to about 34MB for the same session, a 96% reduction, because the overwhelming majority of samples in a real workload retrace a small number of hot paths.
slots.label: Profiling data as a fourth signal: storing stack traces as flame-graph deltas

slots.sample: Merging profiles across pods for a service view
slots.label: Profiling data as a fourth signal: storing stack traces as flame-graph deltas

slots.sample: A service-level flame graph query has to merge call trees from potentially hundreds of pod-level profiling sessions. Because each pod's call tree uses semantically identical function names (from the same binary or interpreter), merging is a tree-union operation keyed by function symbol rather than a raw byte-level merge — on a 200-pod service, this merge for a 1-hour window completes in about 380ms.
slots.label: Profiling data as a fourth signal: storing stack traces as flame-graph deltas

slots.sample: What this means for adoption cost
slots.label: Profiling data as a fourth signal: storing stack traces as flame-graph deltas

slots.sample: Because storage cost per sampled second is so much lower than naive encoding would suggest, we default continuous profiling to always-on at 10ms resolution rather than the opt-in, sampled-window approach some other profilers use — a design decision that only holds up economically because of the delta encoding described here.
slots.label: Profiling data as a fourth signal: storing stack traces as flame-graph deltas

slots.sample: Stack samples are stored as references into a shared call-tree, not independent frame lists.
slots.label: Profiling data as a fourth signal: storing stack traces as flame-graph deltas

slots.sample: Measured storage reduction on a representative session: 96% (890MB to 34MB) versus naive flat encoding.
slots.label: Profiling data as a fourth signal: storing stack traces as flame-graph deltas

slots.sample: Service-level flame graph merges across 200 pods complete in about 380ms via symbol-keyed tree union.
slots.label: Profiling data as a fourth signal: storing stack traces as flame-graph deltas

slots.sample: When HelixQL samples instead of scanning everything, how far off can the answer be? We publish the error bound, not just a disclaimer.
slots.label: The math behind our sampling-error bounds for approximate summarize

slots.sample: For very large scans — billions of rows over long time ranges — HelixQL can answer `summarize` queries approximately, using reservoir sampling instead of a full scan, when a query opts into `approx summarize`. The obvious question is how wrong the answer can be, and we think a vague "approximate" label isn't good enough for engineers making decisions during an incident.
slots.label: The math behind our sampling-error bounds for approximate summarize

slots.sample: The sampling method
slots.label: The math behind our sampling-error bounds for approximate summarize

slots.sample: Approximate queries use reservoir sampling at a configurable rate (default targets a 100,000-row sample regardless of source size) uniformly across the scanned chunks, weighted so each chunk contributes proportionally to its row count. This avoids the common failure mode of naive sampling, where a scan that touches unevenly-sized chunks over-represents small, dense time windows.
slots.label: The math behind our sampling-error bounds for approximate summarize

slots.sample: The error bound, concretely
slots.label: The math behind our sampling-error bounds for approximate summarize

slots.sample: For a `count()` aggregation, standard sampling theory gives a relative standard error of roughly 1/sqrt(sample_size) for a uniform random sample, which at our default 100,000-row sample works out to about 0.32% relative error at one standard deviation, or roughly ±0.6% at a 95% confidence level for a well-mixed population. For `p95`/`p99` quantile estimates, the error is wider and depends on the local density of the distribution near that quantile — we compute this per query using the t-digest sketch's own error estimate rather than a fixed constant, since a p99 estimate over a distribution with a sharp cliff is inherently less certain than one over a smooth tail.
slots.label: The math behind our sampling-error bounds for approximate summarize

slots.sample: Why we surface the confidence interval, not just the estimate
slots.label: The math behind our sampling-error bounds for approximate summarize

slots.sample: Every `approx summarize` result carries a `confidence_interval_width` field per group, and low-population groups (a route hit only 40 times in the sampled window, for instance) get a visibly wider interval rather than a falsely precise-looking number. We validated this against ground truth on 20 large historical queries re-run as full scans: 94% of our reported 95% confidence intervals actually contained the true value, close enough to the nominal 95% that we trust the estimator in production.
slots.label: The math behind our sampling-error bounds for approximate summarize

slots.sample: What this means for on-call
slots.label: The math behind our sampling-error bounds for approximate summarize

slots.sample: During an incident, a 30-day approximate query returns in roughly 400ms instead of the 25-40s a full scan over that range would take, with an honestly-labeled error bound instead of a silent one — good enough to say "yes, p95 really did double," even if the exact decimal isn't the one you'd cite in a postmortem.
slots.label: The math behind our sampling-error bounds for approximate summarize

slots.sample: Reservoir sampling targets a 100,000-row sample by default, weighted proportionally across chunks.
slots.label: The math behind our sampling-error bounds for approximate summarize

slots.sample: Count aggregations carry roughly ±0.6% relative error at 95% confidence at the default sample size.
slots.label: The math behind our sampling-error bounds for approximate summarize

slots.sample: Validated against 20 full-scan ground-truth queries: reported 95% confidence intervals were correct 94% of the time.
slots.label: The math behind our sampling-error bounds for approximate summarize

slots.sample: A payment-gateway blip should have been a five-second blip. Instead, client-side retries turned it into an 11-minute checkout outage. Here is the timeline.
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: At 14:02 UTC on January 12th, our payment gateway partner had a 4-second latency spike on their side. By 14:04 our own checkout API was returning 5xx to 60% of requests. The gateway blip lasted seconds. Our outage lasted eleven minutes.
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: Timeline
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: 14:02:10 — upstream payment gateway p99 jumps from 220ms to 4.1s for about 40 seconds. 14:02:41 — our checkout-service client, configured with a 2s timeout and 3 retries with no backoff, starts re-sending the same requests immediately on timeout. 14:03:15 — outbound request volume to the gateway is 6x normal; the gateway starts shedding load and returning 429s, which our client also retries immediately. 14:04:02 — checkout-service's own connection pool (200 connections) is exhausted waiting on retries; new incoming checkout requests start queueing. 14:04:30 — on-call is paged on checkout 5xx rate > 5%. 14:09:00 — responder identifies the retry amplification via HelixQL and disables the retry middleware via feature flag. 14:13:00 — 5xx rate back under 0.5%.
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: Root cause
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: The retry policy had no backoff and no jitter, and worse, it did not distinguish between a timeout (retry-worthy) and a 429 (do-not-retry-immediately). A single 40-second upstream blip turned into a 6x traffic multiplier that outlasted the original problem by 9 minutes because the retries themselves were now the load.
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: The fix
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: We found the amplification pattern by comparing inbound request volume to outbound gateway calls per trace_id — a 1:3 ratio should be rare and a 1:6 ratio should almost never happen outside an incident.
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: That query, re-run against the 14:00–14:15 window, showed the retry ratio crossing 0.55 at 14:03:00 — a full minute before the connection pool exhaustion paged anyone. We capped retries at 2, added exponential backoff with jitter (250ms base), and made 429 responses non-retryable for 5 seconds via a client-side circuit breaker.
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: What changed
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: We now alert directly on retry_ratio > 0.3 sustained for 20 seconds on any service, which would have paged us a full minute earlier than the 5xx-rate alert did. We also added a standing HelixQL saved query, "retry-amplification," to the on-call dashboard so responders don't have to write it from scratch under pressure.
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: Cap client retries at 2 with exponential backoff and jitter on all payment-path services.
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: Treat HTTP 429 as non-retryable for a cooldown window, not an automatic retry trigger.
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: Alert on retry_ratio > 0.3, not just downstream error rate — it fires earlier.
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: Load-test the retry policy itself during game days, not just the happy path.
slots.label: The retry storm that took checkout down for eleven minutes

slots.sample: Not every retro is about what went wrong. This one is about what went right: a bad deploy caught and rolled back in under nine minutes end to end.
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: On January 16th a routine deploy to notification-service shipped a broken readiness probe. Total customer impact: nine minutes, and only on retried background jobs. We think it's worth writing up precisely because it went well.
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: Timeline
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: 10:41:00 — v2.44.0 of notification-service rolls out to 20% of pods via canary. 10:41:30 — the new build's readiness endpoint returns 500 because of an unhandled nil config value, but the pods stay in the load balancer for 30 seconds past the failed check due to a slow deregistration setting. 10:42:00 — error rate on notification-service crosses 8%, our SLO burn-rate alert fires (2% of the 30-day error budget in under 5 minutes). 10:42:40 — on-call Lena is paged, opens the incident channel, and pulls up the deploy timeline panel. 10:44:10 — she confirms the correlation between the v2.44.0 rollout marker and the error spike using HelixQL, and triggers rollback. 10:45:50 — canary pods are drained and replaced with v2.43.1. 10:49:30 — error rate back to baseline.
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: Root cause
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: A config struct that used to be populated by a required environment variable silently defaulted to nil when we switched to a new config-loading library two sprints earlier. It only surfaced when the readiness probe path touched that specific field, which the pre-deploy smoke tests didn't exercise.
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: The fix
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: The burn-rate alert is what made this fast — it fired on budget consumption velocity, not a static error-rate threshold, so it caught the spike in under 90 seconds. The confirming query took 90 more seconds:
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: The output made the v2.44.0-only error spike undeniable, which meant no debate, no "let's watch it for a few more minutes" — just rollback.
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: What changed
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: We added a required-field validation step to the config loader's startup path so a nil-default fails fast at boot instead of at first use, and we shortened canary deregistration from 30s to 5s.
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: Burn-rate alerts beat static thresholds for catching bad deploys fast — keep tuning them, not replacing them.
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: Keep a one-query "what changed in the last 10 minutes" HelixQL saved search on every service dashboard.
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: Fail-fast config validation at boot, not at first access.
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: Shorten canary deregistration windows; 30 seconds is too long to matter at this traffic volume.
slots.label: Five minutes to detect, four to fix: anatomy of a fast MTTR

slots.sample: A schema migration dropped an index nobody remembered was load-bearing. Postgres started sequential-scanning a 40-million-row table, and the whole orders service crawled.
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: At 11:15 on January 21st, a migration meant to rename a column on the orders table quietly dropped and recreated it without its composite index. p95 latency on order-lookup went from 45ms to 6.8 seconds in under two minutes.
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: Timeline
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: 11:15:00 — migration 0187_rename_customer_ref runs during the deploy window; it uses a generic "add column, backfill, drop old column" pattern that doesn't explicitly recreate indexes on the old column. 11:16:40 — order-lookup p95 crosses 2s, our SLO alert for the orders service fires. 11:18:00 — on-call Priya confirms via HelixQL that latency correlates exactly with the migration completion timestamp, not with any code deploy. 11:21:00 — EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the slow query confirms a sequential scan on a 40M-row table. 11:24:00 — team decides against a rollback (data was already backfilled) and instead runs CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. 11:47:00 — index build completes; p95 drops to 52ms within 90 seconds as query plans flip back to index scans.
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: Root cause
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: Our migration tooling recreates columns but does not carry forward indexes automatically, and the migration's own review checklist didn't have an explicit "list indexes on this table before and after" step. The 26-minute gap between detection and full recovery was the CONCURRENTLY index build itself, which we chose over a lock-and-block rebuild specifically to avoid a second outage.
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: The fix
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: The query that nailed the correlation to the exact migration, not the deploy:
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: Cross-referencing that jump against the migration log's exact commit timestamp (11:15:42) versus the last code deploy (10:40:00, unrelated) told us within three minutes this was a schema problem, not an application one — which saved us from wasting time bisecting application code.
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: What changed
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: Migrations that touch indexed columns on tables over 1M rows now require an explicit index-diff in the PR description and a dry run against a production-sized snapshot in staging. We also added a HelixQL alert that fires when a table's sequential-scan ratio jumps more than 10x in a 5-minute window, independent of latency thresholds.
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: Require an explicit before/after index diff on any migration touching a table over 1M rows.
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: Dry-run schema migrations against a production-sized data snapshot, not a small staging table.
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: Alert on sequential-scan ratio jumps, which catch this class of bug before latency does.
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: Default to CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in the runbook so responders don't have to decide under pressure.
slots.label: The missing index that turned a routine deploy into a forty-minute outage

slots.sample: This wasn't a single incident — it was three weeks of chasing a slow, creeping p95 regression on checkout until we found the connection-pool bug underneath it.
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: Checkout API p95 crept from 180ms to 310ms over three weeks in late January. No single deploy caused it, no alert fired, and it took a dedicated push to find and fix — bringing p95 back to 165ms, a 40%+ improvement over where it started.
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: Timeline
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: Week of Jan 5 — p95 sits at 180ms, stable. Week of Jan 12 — p95 drifts to 240ms; nothing pages because the SLO threshold is 400ms and error rate is unaffected. Jan 22 — a customer support ticket about "slow checkout" prompts Arjun to pull up the 30-day p95 trend and notice the drift. Jan 24 — team starts a focused investigation. Jan 26 — root cause identified: connection pool checkout wait time, not query time, is the growing component. Jan 28 — fix ships; p95 lands at 165ms.
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: Root cause
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: Our database connection pool was sized for a traffic pattern from eight months earlier. As we'd added two new checkout-adjacent services that also queried the same database, total concurrent connection demand had grown past the pool's max size, and requests were queueing for a connection before they ever issued a query.
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: That query, run over the full 30-day window, showed pool-acquire p95 climbing from 8ms to 140ms — almost the entire regression was sitting in the "waiting for a connection" span, invisible if you only looked at query duration.
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: The fix
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: We separated the shared database into per-service connection pools with PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode, raised the effective connection ceiling, and added explicit pool-utilization metrics per service. We also right-sized pool max based on measured p99 concurrent query count rather than a round number someone picked at launch.
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: What changed
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: The real lesson wasn't the pool sizing — it was that we had no alert on pool-acquire wait time, so a 17x regression grew for three weeks under an SLO that only watched total latency. We now track pool-acquire p95 as its own SLI with its own burn-rate alert, separate from end-to-end request latency.
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: Break end-to-end latency into its component spans and alert on each one, not just the total.
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: Size connection pools against measured concurrent demand, revisited quarterly, not a launch-day guess.
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: A support ticket is a valid incident trigger — don't wait for a threshold breach.
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: Per-service pooling isolates noisy neighbors from sharing one starved connection budget.
slots.label: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro

slots.sample: Cutting p95 by 40% on the checkout API: the full retro
