slots.sample: An SLO is a query, a target, and a burn rate, nothing more exotic than that. Build the first one on the metric your users would actually notice.
slots.label: Setting up your first SLO in Helix

slots.sample: The hardest part of a first SLO is rarely the tooling, it is picking the right indicator. Pick something a user would notice breaking, not something convenient to measure, and the rest of the setup is close to mechanical.
slots.label: Setting up your first SLO in Helix

slots.sample: 1. Choose an indicator users would feel
slots.label: Setting up your first SLO in Helix

slots.sample: For a request-driven service, the standard choice is the ratio of fast-enough, successful requests to total requests. Resist the temptation to start with something internal like queue depth, that measures the system, not the experience.
slots.label: Setting up your first SLO in Helix

slots.sample: 2. Set the target from history, not from ambition
slots.label: Setting up your first SLO in Helix

slots.sample: Query the last ninety days of the indicator above before choosing a number. A target of 99.9 percent means very little if the service has never sustained better than 99.5 percent, it just guarantees the SLO starts life already burned.
slots.label: Setting up your first SLO in Helix

slots.sample: 3. Define the error budget and the burn-rate alert
slots.label: Setting up your first SLO in Helix

slots.sample: A 99.9 percent monthly target leaves roughly 43 minutes of budget. The useful alert is not "the SLO breached", by the time that fires it is too late to matter, it is a fast-burn alert that catches the budget being consumed at a rate that would exhaust it early.
slots.label: Setting up your first SLO in Helix

slots.sample: 4. Put the budget on a dashboard, not just in an alert
slots.label: Setting up your first SLO in Helix

slots.sample: A team that only hears about the SLO when it pages will treat every burn-rate alert as an emergency. A visible budget-remaining panel, checked in a weekly review, turns the same signal into a planning input instead of a fire drill.
slots.label: Setting up your first SLO in Helix

slots.sample: Base the indicator on something a user would notice, not an internal system metric.
slots.label: Setting up your first SLO in Helix

slots.sample: Set the target from ninety days of real history, not from an aspirational number.
slots.label: Setting up your first SLO in Helix

slots.sample: Alert on burn rate, not on breach, so there is time to act before the budget is gone.
slots.label: Setting up your first SLO in Helix

slots.sample: Review the remaining budget weekly as a planning input, not only during incidents.
slots.label: Setting up your first SLO in Helix

slots.sample: A dashboard edited by hand in the UI drifts silently. Defining it as a JSON file in a repo turns every change into a reviewable diff.
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: Dashboards built entirely in the UI have no history. Nobody can say why a panel query changed six months ago, and restoring a deleted dashboard means rebuilding it from memory. Treating the definition as a file checked into a repository fixes both problems at once.
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: 1. Export an existing dashboard as JSON
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: Every Helix dashboard has an underlying JSON definition, panels, queries, layout, and variables, reachable from the export action or the CLI. Pull it down as the starting point rather than writing one from scratch.
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: 2. Parameterize the parts that repeat
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: Most teams end up with near-identical dashboards per service, differing only in the service name and a couple of custom panels. A small templating layer turns one JSON file into a generator for all of them.
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: 3. Apply through CI, not through the UI
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: Once a dashboard lives as a file, the deploy step is a CLI call. Wiring it into the same pipeline that ships application code means a dashboard change goes through the same review a config change would.
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: 4. Detect drift between the repo and production
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: Someone will still edit a dashboard directly in the UI during an incident, and that is fine in the moment. What matters is catching it afterward, a scheduled CI job that diffs the live definition against the repo version turns silent drift into a visible pull request.
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: The point of dashboards as code is not purity, it is that a broken panel has a git blame instead of a shrug.
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: The first drift check almost always surprises whoever runs it. It is common to find two or three dashboards that were edited live during an old incident and never reconciled back into the repo, quietly diverging further with every UI edit since. Reconciling those once, rather than starting the drift job from a clean slate, is worth doing before turning the check on for good.
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: Export existing dashboards as JSON before writing any new ones by hand.
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: Template the parts that repeat across services instead of copy-pasting whole definitions.
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: Apply changes through CI so dashboard edits go through the same review as code.
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: Run a scheduled drift check between the repo and what is actually live.
slots.label: Dashboards as code: version-controlling your Helix views

slots.sample: Cardinality problems are invisible until the bill or the query latency makes them obvious. A budget catches the runaway label before either happens.
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: A metric with a user ID or a request ID as a label dimension does not look dangerous when it is added. It looks dangerous three weeks later, when the number of distinct time series has grown past a million and every dashboard querying it has gotten noticeably slower to load.
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: 1. Measure cardinality per metric before it becomes a problem
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: Helix tracks the distinct series count for every metric automatically. Query it directly rather than waiting to notice a slow dashboard, that is usually the first symptom, not the first cause.
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: 2. Set a budget per metric, not one number for the whole account
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: A single account-wide cardinality limit either blocks a legitimate high-cardinality metric or lets a runaway one through unchecked. Budgets scoped per metric name catch the actual offender.
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: 3. Find the label actually driving the growth
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: When a budget alert fires, the useful next step is not deleting the metric, it is identifying which single label dimension is responsible, so only that one gets dropped or bucketed.
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: Nine times out of ten this points at exactly one label, a user ID, a session token, a raw URL path with an embedded ID, that has no business being a metric dimension. Removing that one label, and moving the detail it carried into a trace attribute instead, usually resolves the entire budget breach without losing any real diagnostic value.
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: 4. Review budgets quarterly, not just when they break
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: A metric that was safely under budget at launch can drift as a product adds features and label values multiply. A quarterly review of the top twenty metrics by series count catches slow drift before it becomes an incident.
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: Query distinct series count per metric before a slow dashboard forces the question.
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: Set budgets per metric name, not a single account-wide ceiling.
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: When a budget breaks, find the offending label dimension before deleting anything.
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: Review the top series-count metrics quarterly, cardinality drifts, it rarely spikes without warning.
slots.label: Setting a cardinality budget before it sets you

slots.sample: Head-based sampling decides before a request finishes. Tail-based sampling waits, and keeps the traces that turned out to matter. Here is how to enable it for one service.
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: Head-based sampling makes the keep-or-drop decision at the start of a request, before anyone knows whether it will fail or run slow. That means a flat ten percent sample rate keeps ten percent of the failures too, exactly the traces most worth keeping at one hundred percent. Tail-based sampling fixes this by deciding at the end instead.
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: 1. Route traces through the sampling collector
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: Tail-based sampling needs to see a complete trace before deciding, which means buffering spans for a window rather than exporting them immediately. Point the service at a collector configured for tail sampling instead of exporting directly to Helix.
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: 2. Order the policies deliberately
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: Tail sampling policies evaluate in order, and the first matching policy decides the outcome for that trace. Put the always-keep rules, errors and high latency, ahead of the probabilistic catch-all, or a percentage rule evaluated first can discard a trace that a later error rule would have kept.
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: 3. Watch the decision-wait window against real latency
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: The collector cannot make a keep-or-drop decision until it has seen the trace finish, or until the wait window expires, whichever comes first. Set
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: comfortably above the slowest normal request for the service, or genuinely slow-but-fine requests will get cut off mid-trace and evaluated as incomplete.
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: If p99 duration is close to the configured
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: , raise the window before enabling the policy in production.
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: 4. Confirm the sample rate landed where expected
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: After a day of traffic, check the actual kept percentage against the intended one, tail sampling configuration is easy to get subtly wrong, and the only reliable way to know it worked is to measure it.
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: Keep one hundred percent of errors and slow requests, sample the rest at a lower rate.
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: Order policies with always-keep rules first, the probabilistic catch-all last.
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: Set
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: above the p99 duration for the service, not below it.
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: Measure the actual kept percentage after enabling, do not assume the config did what it says.
slots.label: Turning on tail-based sampling for a single service

slots.sample: A latency histogram tells you p99 jumped. An exemplar tells you which trace produced that outlier point, without a separate search.
slots.label: Wiring exemplars from a metric back to a trace

slots.sample: Staring at a spike on a latency histogram and then manually searching traces for one that roughly matches the timestamp is slow and imprecise, especially on a service handling thousands of requests per second. Exemplars attach an actual trace ID to individual histogram buckets, so the spike points directly at the request that caused it.
slots.label: Wiring exemplars from a metric back to a trace

slots.sample: 1. Enable exemplar recording on the histogram
slots.label: Wiring exemplars from a metric back to a trace

slots.sample: By default the SDK records histogram buckets without exemplars, since storing a trace reference per bucket costs slightly more overhead. Turn it on explicitly for the metrics worth this level of detail.
slots.label: Wiring exemplars from a metric back to a trace

slots.sample: 2. Query the histogram with exemplars attached
slots.label: Wiring exemplars from a metric back to a trace

slots.sample: Exemplars ride along with the metric data itself, retrievable in the same query rather than a separate call.
slots.label: Wiring exemplars from a metric back to a trace

slots.sample: 3. Jump straight from chart to trace
slots.label: Wiring exemplars from a metric back to a trace

slots.sample: In the Helix UI, any histogram panel built with exemplar-enabled data shows small markers on outlier points. Clicking one opens the exact trace behind that data point directly, no copying a trace ID between tabs, no guessing which request in a time window matches the spike.
slots.label: Wiring exemplars from a metric back to a trace

slots.sample: 4. Reserve it for the metrics that page
slots.label: Wiring exemplars from a metric back to a trace

slots.sample: Exemplar recording adds a small amount of memory overhead per histogram, and turning it on for every metric in a large service is unnecessary. Enable it specifically for the handful of latency and error-rate metrics that already have alerts attached, those are the ones someone will actually click through during an incident.
slots.label: Wiring exemplars from a metric back to a trace

slots.sample: An exemplar is not a replacement for tracing, it is a bookmark. It only works because full tracing was already in place to bookmark into.
slots.label: Wiring exemplars from a metric back to a trace

slots.sample: Teams that adopt exemplars usually notice the same pattern within the first week: the outlier points on a histogram are rarely random. A cluster of exemplars pointing at the same slow downstream call, or the same customer account with an unusually large cart, turns a vague latency spike into a specific, fixable cause far faster than paging through raw traces in the hope of stumbling onto the right one.
slots.label: Wiring exemplars from a metric back to a trace

slots.sample: Turn on exemplar recording explicitly, it is off by default for overhead reasons.
slots.label: Wiring exemplars from a metric back to a trace

slots.sample: alongside the metric to pull the backing trace directly.

slots.sample: A dozen services should not all page the same catch-all channel. Route by ownership metadata baked into the alert rule itself, not a manual triage step.
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: The default failure mode for a growing alert set is everything landing in one channel, followed by a human deciding who should actually own each page. That triage step is slow exactly when speed matters most. Routing on ownership metadata at alert-creation time removes it entirely.
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: 1. Tag ownership at the source
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: Ownership belongs on the service, not on the alert rule, so it stays correct even as alert rules are added and removed. Set it as a resource attribute at SDK initialization, the same place service name and environment are already set.
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: 2. Reference the attribute in the alert notify clause
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: Instead of hard-coding a destination in every alert rule, resolve it dynamically from the same attribute set on the traced service, so a new alert on an existing service routes correctly without any extra configuration.
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: 3. Fall back to a default owner, never to nothing
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: Services occasionally ship without the ownership attribute set, usually a new one still under active development. Configure a fallback destination for anything missing the tag, so a gap in metadata produces a page to a platform team rather than an alert that silently has nowhere to go.
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: 4. Audit ownership coverage on a schedule
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: Ownership tags drift as teams reorganize and services change hands. A monthly query listing every service with either a missing owner tag or an owner tag pointing at a paging integration that no longer exists catches the gap before an incident does.
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: This audit is worth running as a scheduled job rather than a manual quarterly task, since the cost of finding a stale route during an actual incident is far higher than the cost of a query that runs itself every month. A service silently paging a defunct integration looks identical to a healthy alert setup right up until it is needed.
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: Set ownership as a resource attribute on the service, not inside each alert rule.
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: Resolve the paging destination dynamically from that attribute in the notify clause.
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: Always define a fallback route for services missing the ownership tag.
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: Audit ownership coverage on a monthly schedule, tags drift as teams reorganize.
slots.label: Routing alerts by service owner with HelixQL

slots.sample: CPU and memory profiles usually get pulled manually, after something is already on fire. Continuous profiling keeps them running in the background for free.
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: The typical profiling workflow is reactive: something is slow, someone runs
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: by hand, captures thirty seconds of data, and hopes the problem happened to occur during that window. Continuous profiling removes the timing gamble by sampling constantly at low overhead and keeping history to query later.
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: 1. Add the profiler alongside existing instrumentation
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: The Helix Go SDK ships a profiler package that runs on its own goroutine and samples at a low, fixed rate designed to stay under one percent CPU overhead in steady state.
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: 2. Correlate a profile with a specific slow trace
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: The real value shows up when a profile can be scoped to the exact time window of a slow request, rather than a generic five-minute average across all traffic.
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: 3. Compare before and after a deploy
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: Because profiles are continuous rather than one-off snapshots, comparing CPU time by function across two deploy versions is a straightforward filter rather than a manual before-and-after capture.
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: A function that jumps from a small share of total CPU time to a dominant one between two adjacent versions is usually the fastest way to catch a performance regression before it shows up as a latency alert three days later.
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: 4. Keep retention shorter than traces
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: Profile data is bulky relative to traces. A retention window of seven to fourteen days is usually enough, since profiling is almost always used to investigate something recent, not to answer a question from three months ago.
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: Add the profiler at startup, the same low-overhead pattern as trace and metric setup.
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: Scope profile queries to the time window of a specific slow trace for precise answers.
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: Compare CPU time by function across deploy versions to catch regressions early.
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: Set a shorter retention window for profiles than for traces, recent history is what matters.
slots.label: Turning on continuous profiling for a Go service

slots.sample: You do not have to send telemetry directly from every service. Running a Collector in front of Helix buys batching, retry, and a place to enforce sampling in one spot.
slots.label: Configuring the OpenTelemetry Collector for Helix

slots.sample: Every Helix SDK can export directly to the platform, and for a single small service that is often the right amount of infrastructure. Past a handful of services, a shared OpenTelemetry Collector in front of Helix earns its keep by centralizing batching, retry, and sampling policy instead of duplicating it in every application.
slots.label: Configuring the OpenTelemetry Collector for Helix

slots.sample: 1. Start with the minimum viable pipeline
slots.label: Configuring the OpenTelemetry Collector for Helix

slots.sample: A collector configuration is three sections: receivers accept data in, processors transform it, exporters send it out. The smallest useful configuration for Helix needs exactly one of each.
slots.label: Configuring the OpenTelemetry Collector for Helix

slots.sample: 2. Add a memory limiter before anything else
slots.label: Configuring the OpenTelemetry Collector for Helix

slots.sample: Without a bound on buffered data, a collector under a sudden traffic spike or a temporarily unreachable Helix endpoint will happily consume memory until the process is killed by the OS, taking the telemetry pipeline for every service behind it down at once.
slots.label: Configuring the OpenTelemetry Collector for Helix

slots.sample: 3. Run it as a sidecar in low-traffic environments, a gateway in high-traffic ones
slots.label: Configuring the OpenTelemetry Collector for Helix

slots.sample: For a handful of services, a collector sidecar per pod is simple and isolates failures per service. Past a few dozen services, a dedicated collector gateway tier, deployed and scaled independently, is easier to operate and gives one place to apply account-wide policy like tail sampling.
slots.label: Configuring the OpenTelemetry Collector for Helix

slots.sample: 4. Monitor the collector itself
slots.label: Configuring the OpenTelemetry Collector for Helix

slots.sample: The collector exposes its own internal metrics, queue size, dropped spans, export failures, on a standard endpoint. slots.sample: A log line that is just a formatted string is a log line HelixQL has to parse at query time, every time. A few naming conventions fix that permanently.
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: The difference between a log line that queries in milliseconds and one that requires a regex scan across a week of data usually comes down to whether it was written as structured fields from the start, not whether it was written well.
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: 1. Emit fields, not formatted strings
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: A message like
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: is readable to a person and nearly useless to a query engine. The same information as fields is queryable directly, with no string parsing at all.
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: 2. Keep field names consistent across services
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: If one service logs
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: and another logs
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: or
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: , every cross-service query needs to know and handle all three, which nobody remembers to do under incident pressure. Publish a short naming convention document and treat it the same as an API contract.
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: 3. Put the stable identifier in a field, not just the trace context
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: Trace ID correlation is powerful, but not every useful query starts from a trace. A support engineer investigating one customer complaint wants to filter logs by
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: directly, without first finding a trace ID to join through.
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: 4. Avoid high-cardinality fields as indexed dimensions
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: Structured does not mean every field should be treated as a queryable dimension at the storage layer. Free-text fields like a full stack trace or a raw request body should stay as payload, not become part of the index, or the same cardinality problem that affects metrics shows up in logs too.
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: Emit fields, not formatted message strings, so queries never need to parse text.
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: Standardize field names across services in a short, enforced naming convention.
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: Include stable business identifiers as fields, not only reachable through a trace join.
slots.label: Structured logging conventions that make queries fast

slots.sample: Keep free-text payload out of the indexed dimension set to avoid a cardinality blowup.

slots.sample: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation. Four panels, one query shape each, and a service has a dashboard that answers the first question in almost any incident.
slots.label: Building a golden-signals dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: The golden signals framework is old enough to feel like a cliche, and it earns that reputation by still being the fastest way to answer the first question of any incident: what actually changed. Building the four panels by hand, rather than starting from a template, is worth doing once to understand exactly what each query is doing.
slots.label: Building a golden-signals dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: 1. Latency
slots.label: Building a golden-signals dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Percentiles, not averages, an average latency chart can look perfectly flat while ten percent of users wait five seconds.
slots.label: Building a golden-signals dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: 2. Traffic
slots.label: Building a golden-signals dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Simple request volume, but grouped by route, a flat total line can hide one route silently dropping to zero while another compensates.
slots.label: Building a golden-signals dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: 3. Errors
slots.label: Building a golden-signals dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Rate, not raw count, a raw error count chart makes low-traffic overnight hours look deceptively calm and high-traffic peak hours look deceptively alarming, even at the same underlying failure rate.
slots.label: Building a golden-signals dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: 4. Saturation
slots.label: Building a golden-signals dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: The one signal that does not come from traces. Pull it from infrastructure metrics instead, and pick the resource actually likely to run out first for this specific service, CPU for a compute-bound one, connection pool usage for a database-bound one.
slots.label: Building a golden-signals dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Stack the four panels in that order, latency at the top, saturation at the bottom, and the dashboard reads left to right as a story: what users felt, how much traffic there was, how much of it failed, and what resource was closest to its limit. That ordering is not arbitrary, it mirrors the order most people actually reason through an incident.
slots.label: Building a golden-signals dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Break traffic down by route, a flat total can hide a single dead endpoint.
slots.label: Building a golden-signals dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Chart error rate, not raw error count, so the baseline holds across traffic levels.
slots.label: Building a golden-signals dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Pick the saturation metric that actually matters for this service, not a generic default.

slots.sample: Before reaching for an automated view, it is worth knowing how to build a request timeline manually, trace, logs, and metrics, stitched by hand from HelixQL.
slots.label: Assembling a request timeline from three signal types by hand

slots.sample: Helix has automation that assembles an incident timeline for you. It is worth learning to do it manually first, because understanding what the automation is actually doing under the hood is what makes it trustworthy instead of a black box during a real incident.
slots.label: Assembling a request timeline from three signal types by hand

slots.sample: 1. Anchor on the trace
slots.label: Assembling a request timeline from three signal types by hand

slots.sample: Start with the slow or failed request itself. The trace gives a start time, an end time, and every span in between, which becomes the time window for everything else.
slots.label: Assembling a request timeline from three signal types by hand

slots.sample: 2. Pull logs into that exact window
slots.label: Assembling a request timeline from three signal types by hand

slots.sample: With the trace start and end time in hand, logs from every service involved, not just the one that emitted the trace, can be pulled into the same window for a fuller picture of what else was happening.
slots.label: Assembling a request timeline from three signal types by hand

slots.sample: 3. Overlay the relevant metric
slots.label: Assembling a request timeline from three signal types by hand

slots.sample: A request-level view is incomplete without the system-level context around it, a CPU spike, a connection pool exhausting, a downstream queue backing up, all visible only in metrics, not in the trace or the logs.
slots.label: Assembling a request timeline from three signal types by hand

slots.sample: 4. Lay the three outputs side by side, in order
slots.label: Assembling a request timeline from three signal types by hand

slots.sample: The manual version of this exercise is three separate query results, read in the order above, trace first for the shape of the request, logs second for what was said along the way, metrics third for the surrounding system state. That reading order is exactly what the automated timeline feature does for you once it is trusted, the value of building it by hand once is knowing when to fall back to the manual version, because the automation, like any correlation tool, occasionally misses a boundary case.
slots.label: Assembling a request timeline from three signal types by hand

slots.sample: Anchor the investigation on the trace start and end time, everything else is scoped to that window.
slots.label: Assembling a request timeline from three signal types by hand

slots.sample: Pull logs from every service in the request path, not only the one that failed.
slots.label: Assembling a request timeline from three signal types by hand

slots.sample: Overlay system metrics for the same window to see resource context the trace cannot show.
slots.label: Assembling a request timeline from three signal types by hand

slots.sample: Read the three outputs in order: trace shape, logs, then system state.
slots.label: Assembling a request timeline from three signal types by hand

slots.sample: A runbook nobody can find during an incident might as well not exist. Link it from the alert itself, and structure it so it is useful at 3am.
slots.label: Writing runbooks your alerts can actually link to

slots.sample: A wiki full of runbooks written months ago, in a folder nobody on the current on-call rotation remembers exists, provides close to zero value during an actual page. The fix is not writing better runbooks, it is making the existing ones reachable in one click from the alert that would need them.
slots.label: Writing runbooks your alerts can actually link to

slots.sample: 1. Attach the runbook URL to the alert rule directly
slots.label: Writing runbooks your alerts can actually link to

slots.sample: Every Helix alert rule has a
slots.label: Writing runbooks your alerts can actually link to

slots.sample: field, included in the page notification itself. An engineer paged at 3am should never have to search for the right document, it should already be one link away in the notification.
slots.label: Writing runbooks your alerts can actually link to

slots.sample: 2. Structure it for a stressed reader, not a calm one
slots.label: Writing runbooks your alerts can actually link to

slots.sample: The first thing a runbook should answer is not background context, it is what to check first. Lead with the diagnostic query, not a paragraph explaining what the service does.
slots.label: Writing runbooks your alerts can actually link to

slots.sample: 3. Link runbooks to each other, not just to the alert
slots.label: Writing runbooks your alerts can actually link to

slots.sample: Incidents rarely stay within the boundary of a single alert. A runbook that ends with a pointer to the two or three most likely follow-on runbooks saves the second lookup that would otherwise happen mid-incident under pressure.
slots.label: Writing runbooks your alerts can actually link to

slots.sample: 4. Treat a stale runbook as a bug, not as documentation debt
slots.label: Writing runbooks your alerts can actually link to

slots.sample: A runbook that references a dashboard which no longer exists, or a query field that got renamed in a schema change, is actively harmful, it wastes the exact minutes an on-call engineer cannot spare. Review runbooks whenever the alert or dashboard they reference changes, not on a separate documentation cadence that nobody prioritizes under deadline pressure.
slots.label: Writing runbooks your alerts can actually link to

slots.label: Writing runbooks your alerts can actually link to

slots.sample: Lead with the first diagnostic query, not background explanation, for a reader under pressure.
slots.label: Writing runbooks your alerts can actually link to

slots.sample: Cross-link related runbooks so a second lookup is not needed mid-incident.

slots.sample: Helix bills primarily on ingest volume. A handful of self-service queries turn a surprising invoice into a predictable, service-attributable line item.
slots.label: Querying your own ingest cost before the invoice does

slots.sample: The first time a Helix invoice jumps noticeably, the natural question is which team caused it, and the natural answer, guessing from memory which service shipped a big feature that month, is almost always wrong. The platform meters its own ingest volume, and that metering is queryable the same way any other signal is.
slots.label: Querying your own ingest cost before the invoice does

slots.sample: 1. Break ingest volume down by service
slots.label: Querying your own ingest cost before the invoice does

slots.sample: Every signal carries its own byte-size metadata internally. Summing it grouped by service turns a vague monthly total into an attributable list.
slots.label: Querying your own ingest cost before the invoice does

slots.sample: 2. Break it down again by signal type
slots.label: Querying your own ingest cost before the invoice does

slots.sample: A service can be expensive for very different reasons, a chatty logging habit versus an unusually high trace volume versus a wide, high-cardinality metric set. The fix differs completely depending on which one it is, so do not stop at the service-level total.
slots.label: Querying your own ingest cost before the invoice does

slots.sample: 3. Track the trend, not just the current snapshot
slots.label: Querying your own ingest cost before the invoice does

slots.sample: A single point-in-time cost query answers "who is expensive right now" but misses a slow, steady climb that will matter far more by the end of the quarter than any single day's number.
slots.label: Querying your own ingest cost before the invoice does

slots.sample: 4. Set a budget alert the same way you would for latency
slots.label: Querying your own ingest cost before the invoice does

slots.sample: Cost is a metric like any other in Helix, and it takes the same alerting mechanics as a latency SLO does, a threshold and a burn rate, just measured in bytes instead of milliseconds.
slots.label: Querying your own ingest cost before the invoice does

slots.sample: Query ingest volume by service before assuming which team caused an invoice jump.
slots.label: Querying your own ingest cost before the invoice does

slots.sample: Break it down further by signal type, the fix differs between logs, traces, and metrics.
slots.label: Querying your own ingest cost before the invoice does

slots.sample: Track the trend over weeks, not just a single snapshot, to catch a slow climb early.
slots.label: Querying your own ingest cost before the invoice does

slots.sample: Set a cost budget alert with the same mechanics as any latency or error-rate alert.
slots.label: Querying your own ingest cost before the invoice does

slots.sample: PromQL and HelixQL solve overlapping problems with different syntax. A direct mental mapping gets most dashboards translated in an afternoon, not a rewrite.
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: Teams migrating off Prometheus usually expect the hardest part to be the query language. It is not, once the mapping between the two clicks, the actual work is deciding which dashboards are still worth keeping rather than quietly retiring.
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: 1. Map the core functions directly
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: Most PromQL rate and aggregation functions have a near one-to-one HelixQL equivalent, just written left to right instead of nested.
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: 2. Replace label matchers with where clauses
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: PromQL label selectors in curly braces become ordinary
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: clauses, with the same regex and negative-match support most PromQL dashboards rely on.
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: 3. Do not migrate recording rules one-to-one
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: Prometheus recording rules exist largely to work around the query engine having to recompute expensive aggregations on every dashboard load. HelixQL's query planner caches and pushes down aggregations automatically, so most recording rules can simply become the equivalent live query rather than a separately maintained pre-computation.
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: The rules worth keeping as a separate scheduled job are the few that feed a long-window rollup, a thirty-day trailing average used in a capacity report, for instance, where recomputing from raw data on every load would be wasteful regardless of how good the planner is. Everything else is simpler as a live query maintained in one place instead of two.
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: 4. Run both in parallel before cutting over
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: For any dashboard feeding an SLO or a paging alert, run the HelixQL version alongside the existing Prometheus one for at least a full week before switching the alert rule over. The two systems compute percentiles slightly differently at the edges, close enough that it rarely matters, different enough that a threshold tuned against one can occasionally behave differently against the other.
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: Map rate and aggregation functions directly, the shape translates left to right.
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: Replace label matchers with ordinary
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: clauses, including regex matches.
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: Drop most recording rules, HelixQL's planner handles the aggregation cost automatically.
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: Run new and old dashboards in parallel for a week before cutting over any alert rule.
slots.label: Migrating dashboards from Prometheus to HelixQL

slots.sample: A single global latency chart hides regional problems in the average. Build one dashboard that makes region-by-region health obvious at a glance.
slots.label: Building a follow-the-sun dashboard for multi-region services

slots.sample: A service running in four regions with one region silently degraded looks completely healthy on a dashboard that only shows the global average, the three healthy regions pull the number back down into a range nobody would flag. Splitting every panel by region fixes that, and it costs one extra field in the group-by clause.
slots.label: Building a follow-the-sun dashboard for multi-region services

slots.sample: 1. Add region to every group-by, not just one panel
slots.label: Building a follow-the-sun dashboard for multi-region services

slots.sample: The habit that actually matters here is discipline, not cleverness: every panel on the dashboard, not just the headline one, needs the same regional breakdown, or the exception becomes the blind spot during the next incident.
slots.label: Building a follow-the-sun dashboard for multi-region services

slots.sample: 2. Add a region-comparison panel, not just per-region lines
slots.label: Building a follow-the-sun dashboard for multi-region services

slots.sample: A chart with four overlapping lines is readable when they track together and unreadable the moment one diverges. A dedicated panel showing the spread between the best and worst region makes the divergence itself the metric, easier to alert on than eyeballing four lines.
slots.label: Building a follow-the-sun dashboard for multi-region services

slots.sample: 3. Account for the follow-the-sun traffic shape itself
slots.label: Building a follow-the-sun dashboard for multi-region services

slots.sample: Regional traffic volume rises and falls on its own daily cycle as usage follows daylight hours. A raw request-count panel per region will look like a false alarm every single day at the same local time unless the on-call rotation for that region already expects the shape and reads past it.
slots.label: Building a follow-the-sun dashboard for multi-region services

slots.sample: 4. Hand the dashboard off with the rotation
slots.label: Building a follow-the-sun dashboard for multi-region services

slots.sample: For a follow-the-sun on-call model, the dashboard itself should be part of the handoff, not just a link. The outgoing region calls out anything currently sitting at the edge of normal before the next region picks up, using the exact panels above as the shared vocabulary for that conversation.
slots.label: Building a follow-the-sun dashboard for multi-region services

slots.sample: Break every panel down by region, not only the headline latency chart.
slots.label: Building a follow-the-sun dashboard for multi-region services

slots.sample: Add a spread panel that turns divergence between regions into a single alertable number.
slots.label: Building a follow-the-sun dashboard for multi-region services

slots.sample: Expect and read past the natural daily traffic cycle per region before calling it an anomaly.
slots.label: Building a follow-the-sun dashboard for multi-region services

slots.sample: Use the dashboard itself as the shared language during a follow-the-sun handoff.

slots.sample: A good handoff answers three questions before anyone asks them. Build the dashboard around those three questions instead of a generic service overview.
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Most handoff dashboards are just the standard service overview reused for a different purpose, and it shows, half the panels answer questions nobody asks during a handoff. A purpose-built one starts from the three questions an incoming on-call engineer actually needs answered, then builds exactly one panel per question.
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: 1. What is currently open
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: The first question is never about historical trends, it is about anything currently unresolved. Pull open alerts directly rather than making the incoming engineer search a separate paging tool.
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: 2. What changed in the last shift
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: A deploy, a config change, or a feature flag flip in the last eight hours is the single most common root cause of anything that happens in the next eight. Surface it explicitly rather than assuming the incoming engineer will think to check.
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: 3. What is trending toward a problem
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Not every risk fires an alert yet. A panel showing SLO burn rate and cardinality growth over the last shift catches the thing that will page the next person if left unaddressed, giving the incoming engineer a chance to get ahead of it.
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: 4. Keep it to three panels, resist adding more
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: The temptation with any handoff dashboard is to keep adding panels for completeness. Resist it, a handoff that takes ten minutes to review does not happen consistently, three focused panels that get read every single time beat twelve comprehensive ones that get skimmed once and then ignored.
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Lead with currently open alerts, pulled directly, not a link to a separate tool.
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Surface every deploy and config change from the last shift explicitly.
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Add a trending-toward-trouble panel for burn rate and cardinality, not just current state.
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Cap it at three panels, a handoff dashboard that takes ten minutes will stop getting read.
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch
slots.label: Building an on-call handoff dashboard from scratch

slots.sample: Assertions on response codes miss a service that got slower or started calling a downstream it should not. Trace-based tests catch the shape of a request, not just its outcome.
slots.label: Writing a trace-based test for your checkout flow

slots.sample: A conventional integration test checks that a checkout request returns a 200 with the right body. It says nothing about whether that request quietly started fanning out to three downstream services instead of one, or whether a step that used to take 40ms now takes 400ms. Trace-based testing asserts on the shape of the request, not only its final outcome.
slots.label: Writing a trace-based test for your checkout flow

slots.sample: 1. Run the flow and capture its trace
slots.label: Writing a trace-based test for your checkout flow

slots.sample: Trigger the checkout flow in a test environment exactly as a normal integration test would, but instead of asserting only on the HTTP response, pull the resulting trace by its ID immediately afterward.
slots.label: Writing a trace-based test for your checkout flow

slots.sample: 2. Assert on span structure, not just span count
slots.label: Writing a trace-based test for your checkout flow

slots.sample: The useful assertions are structural: which services were called, in what order, and whether any span exceeded a duration budget. A span count alone does not catch a call moving from a fast path to a slow one.
slots.label: Writing a trace-based test for your checkout flow

slots.sample: 3. Catch accidental fan-out before it ships
slots.label: Writing a trace-based test for your checkout flow

slots.sample: The last assertion above is the one that catches the most expensive class of regression: a refactor that accidentally reintroduces a call to a deprecated service, or an N+1 pattern that turns one downstream call into a dozen. Neither shows up in a response-code assertion, both show up immediately in the span list.
slots.label: Writing a trace-based test for your checkout flow

slots.sample: 4. Run it in CI against a real, traced environment
slots.label: Writing a trace-based test for your checkout flow

slots.sample: This only works if the test environment is genuinely instrumented, not a set of mocks, since the entire point is observing real inter-service behavior. Run trace-based tests as a distinct CI stage against a staging environment with full instrumentation enabled, separate from the faster unit test suite that runs against mocks.
slots.label: Writing a trace-based test for your checkout flow

slots.sample: Assert on trace structure, service call graph and per-span duration, not only the HTTP response.
slots.label: Writing a trace-based test for your checkout flow

slots.sample: Catch accidental fan-out and deprecated downstream calls that a status-code test cannot see.
slots.label: Writing a trace-based test for your checkout flow

slots.sample: Run trace-based tests against a genuinely instrumented staging environment, not mocks.
slots.label: Writing a trace-based test for your checkout flow

slots.sample: Keep them as a separate, slower CI stage from the standard unit test suite.
slots.label: Writing a trace-based test for your checkout flow

slots.sample: Most first-draft SLOs die in a spreadsheet nobody opens again. Here is the target-setting process that survived contact with three different teams.
slots.label: The SLO That Finally Stuck: Picking Targets People Actually Believe

slots.sample: Our first SLOs were guesses dressed up as math: 99.9% because it sounded serious, 30-day windows because a blog post said so. Nobody believed them, and nobody paged off them for a year.
slots.label: The SLO That Finally Stuck: Picking Targets People Actually Believe

slots.sample: Start from what users actually noticed
slots.label: The SLO That Finally Stuck: Picking Targets People Actually Believe

slots.sample: We stopped opening with a target and started opening with an incident log. For each of the last six months, we asked: was there a period where users would have filed a complaint, even an informal one in Slack? We counted those windows in minutes, not vibes.
slots.label: The SLO That Finally Stuck: Picking Targets People Actually Believe

slots.sample: That gave us a real baseline: our checkout API had roughly 41 minutes of user-visible badness a month. Not zero. Not the four-and-a-half-minutes-a-month that 99.99% implies. We set the SLO at 99.9%, which allows about 43 minutes — close enough to current reality that the team could hit it without heroics, and tight enough to force fixing the worst offender.
slots.label: The SLO That Finally Stuck: Picking Targets People Actually Believe

slots.sample: Make the SLI boring and specific
slots.label: The SLO That Finally Stuck: Picking Targets People Actually Believe

slots.sample: Vague SLIs ("the API is fast and reliable") produce vague arguments during incidents. We defined ours as a single HelixQL query anyone could run and get the same number.
slots.label: The SLO That Finally Stuck: Picking Targets People Actually Believe

slots.sample: Get sign-off from the people who get paged
slots.label: The SLO That Finally Stuck: Picking Targets People Actually Believe

slots.sample: The SLO went to the on-call rotation before it went to leadership. If the engineers carrying the pager think a target is unreasonable, it will quietly rot the first time it's inconvenient. We ran a 30-minute review where the rotation could veto the number — two of five services had their targets loosened after this step, and adoption jumped because of it, not despite it.
slots.label: The SLO That Finally Stuck: Picking Targets People Actually Believe

slots.sample: Publish the reasoning, not just the number
slots.label: The SLO That Finally Stuck: Picking Targets People Actually Believe

slots.sample: Every SLO doc now carries a short "why this number" section alongside the target itself — the incident baseline it was derived from, the date it was last reviewed, who signed off. Six months later, when someone questions why the target is 99.9% and not 99.95%, the answer already exists in the document instead of requiring someone to reconstruct the reasoning from memory or re-run the original analysis from scratch.
slots.label: The SLO That Finally Stuck: Picking Targets People Actually Believe

slots.sample: Derive the target from a real incident baseline, not an industry benchmark.

slots.sample: Write the SLI as one HelixQL query the whole team can run and trust.

slots.sample: Get the on-call rotation to sign off before publishing the number.

slots.sample: Publish the reasoning behind the target next to the target itself.

slots.sample: Revisit the target after the first quarter — don't treat it as permanent.

slots.sample: A runbook that only makes sense to the person who wrote it isn't a runbook, it's a note to self. Here is the format we standardized on.
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: We audited 40 runbooks and found the same failure mode in 30 of them: they were written by an expert, for an expert, and useless to whoever was actually on call at 3 a.m.
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: Lead with the query that confirms the symptom
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: Every runbook now opens with a copy-pasteable HelixQL query that confirms whether the alert's story is true, before any remediation step. This alone cut false-start remediations by a lot — engineers stopped restarting services based on a hunch and started confirming first.
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: Write steps as commands, not descriptions
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: "Check if the queue is backing up" is not a step. "Run this query, if the value is above 5000, go to step 4" is a step. We rewrote every runbook so each line is either a command to run, a query to check, or an explicit branch — no prose that requires interpretation under stress.
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: Put an owner and a last-verified date at the top
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: Unowned runbooks rot silently — a service gets refactored and the remediation steps quietly stop working, and nobody finds out until an incident. Every runbook now has an owner and a last-verified date; anything unverified for 90 days gets flagged in the weekly reliability review and someone has to either re-verify it or archive it.
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: Test the format on someone who didn't write it
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: Before a runbook is considered done, we hand it to an engineer who has never touched the underlying service and time how long it takes them to reach the correct remediation, purely from the document. If that person gets stuck or has to ask a Slack question to proceed, the runbook fails review and goes back for another pass — the author's fluency with the system doesn't count as evidence the page will work at 3 a.m.
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: Open with a query that confirms the symptom before any remediation.
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: Write steps as commands and explicit branches, not prose.
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: Require an owner and a last-verified date on every runbook.
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: Test every runbook on someone unfamiliar with the service before publishing.
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: Archive or re-verify anything untouched for 90 days.
slots.label: Better Runbooks: Turning Tribal Knowledge Into a Page Anyone Can Run

slots.sample: We cut pages per on-call week from 34 to 6 in one quarter without hiding real problems. Here is the plan, week by week.
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan

slots.sample: Nobody fixes alert fatigue with one afternoon of alert tuning. It took us a structured 90-day plan and a weekly review to get pager volume down without losing signal.
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan

slots.sample: Weeks 1–2: inventory before you touch anything
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan

slots.sample: We pulled every alert that fired in the last quarter and ranked it by fire count and by whether the responder took any action beyond acknowledging it. Alerts that fired often and never led to action were the first target — not because they were wrong, but because they had trained everyone to ignore pages.
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan

slots.sample: Weeks 3–8: fix the alert, not the symptom
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan

slots.sample: For each noisy alert we asked one question: is this a symptom-based alert (users are affected right now) or a cause-based alert (something looks off but might self-heal)? Cause-based alerts got demoted to a dashboard or a ticket, never a page. This was the single biggest volume reduction — roughly 60% of our pages were cause-based alerts wearing a symptom-based badge.
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan

slots.sample: Weeks 9–12: add burn-rate alerts to replace static thresholds
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan

slots.sample: Static thresholds like "CPU over 80% for 5 minutes" page on noise. We replaced the worst offenders with multi-window burn-rate alerts tied to actual SLOs, which only fire when the error budget is genuinely at risk, not when a metric wobbles.
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan

slots.sample: What we tracked to know it was working
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan

slots.sample: We didn't just watch total page count drop — a naive team could hit zero pages by deleting everything, which would be a disaster dressed up as success. Alongside volume we tracked mean time to acknowledge and post-incident survey scores from the rotation each week, and both improved in step with the volume drop, which is what told us we'd removed noise and not signal.
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan

slots.sample: Inventory every alert by fire count and action rate before changing anything.
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan

slots.sample: Separate symptom-based alerts (page) from cause-based alerts (dashboard/ticket).
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan

slots.sample: Replace static thresholds with SLO-based burn-rate alerts where it makes sense.
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan

slots.sample: Track acknowledge time and rotation sentiment alongside volume, not volume alone.
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan

slots.sample: Re-run the inventory query monthly — noise creeps back.
slots.label: Reducing Pager Volume: A 90-Day Plan
