slots.sample: Latency, traffic, errors, and saturation cover most of it — but we found a fifth signal worth dashboarding on every service we own.
slots.label: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four

slots.sample: The four golden signals get you most of the way to knowing whether a service is healthy. The fifth one we added — queue depth trend — caught the failures the other four missed until it was too late.
slots.label: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four

slots.sample: Why saturation alone wasn't enough
slots.label: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four

slots.sample: Saturation as usually defined (CPU, memory, disk) told us a box was busy, not that it was about to fall over. Our worst incidents were preceded by a slowly growing queue backlog for 20–40 minutes while CPU and memory looked completely normal — the work was piling up faster than workers could drain it, and none of the standard four signals showed it clearly.
slots.label: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four

slots.sample: Trend, not level, is the useful part
slots.label: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four

slots.sample: A queue depth of 500 means nothing on its own — it depends on throughput. What matters is the second derivative: is the backlog growing faster than it's draining? We alert on sustained positive slope, not on an absolute depth.
slots.label: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four

slots.sample: Roll it out per service, not org-wide
slots.label: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four

slots.sample: Not every service has a meaningful fifth signal — a stateless read-only API doesn't have a queue to watch. We made the fifth signal a required field in the service catalog ("what is your saturation leading indicator, if any") rather than mandating queue depth everywhere, which forced teams to actually think about their own failure mode instead of copy-pasting a dashboard.
slots.label: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four

slots.sample: A batch-heavy data pipeline picked partition lag as its fifth signal instead of queue depth, and a connection-pooled API picked pool-wait time. None of those would have shown up if we'd mandated one metric name for every service — the value was in the question, not in the specific number.
slots.label: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four

slots.sample: Keep the four golden signals, but ask each service what its leading indicator is.
slots.label: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four

slots.sample: Alert on trend (sustained slope) rather than absolute level for backlog-style signals.
slots.label: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four

slots.sample: Make the fifth signal a required, service-specific field, not a copy-pasted dashboard.
slots.label: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four

slots.sample: Validate the fifth signal against a real past incident before trusting it.
slots.label: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four

slots.sample: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four
slots.label: Golden Signals Plus One: Adding Saturation to the Big Four

slots.sample: Most incident confusion happens before anyone has diagnosed anything — it happens because roles weren't assigned. Here is our first-15-minutes checklist.
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: The difference between a 20-minute incident and a 2-hour one is rarely technical skill. It's usually whether someone claimed the incident commander role in the first five minutes.
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: Declare before you diagnose
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: We used to wait until an issue was "confirmed serious" before declaring an incident, which meant the first 10 minutes were spent debating severity instead of responding. Now anyone can declare, and declaring costs nothing — a declared incident with no real impact gets closed in two minutes. The bar for declaring dropped; the bar for staying open didn't.
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: Three roles, assigned out loud
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: Incident commander, communicator, and one or more responders. The IC does not debug — their job is coordination and decisions, and we've found that ICs who start typing commands into a terminal stop doing the job that actually shortens the incident. The communicator posts status updates on a fixed cadence so responders never have to stop and answer "any update?" in the channel.
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: Timebox the first update
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: Whatever is known or unknown at the 15-minute mark gets posted, even if the honest answer is "we don't know yet, here's what we've ruled out." Silence in the first 15 minutes is what causes stakeholders to start their own side-channel investigation, which then competes with the actual response for the same engineers' attention.
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: Measure the handoff between declaring and assigning
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: We started measuring the gap between an incident being declared and an IC actually being assigned, and found a p95 of over five minutes — not because nobody wanted to lead, but because nobody explicitly claimed the role, so everyone quietly assumed someone else would. Adding a single bot prompt that asks "who is IC?" the moment an incident channel opens cut that gap by more than half.
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: Lower the bar to declare; keep the bar to stay declared.
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: Assign IC, communicator, and responder roles out loud, immediately.
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: The IC coordinates and decides — they don't debug.
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: Post a status update by the 15-minute mark even if it's "still investigating."
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: Track time-to-IC-assignment as its own metric — silence there costs real minutes.
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes
slots.label: Incident Command 101: Who Does What in the First 15 Minutes

slots.sample: We killed our weekly reliability meeting and replaced it with one that has a fixed agenda, a hard 30-minute limit, and produces decisions, not updates.
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: Our old reliability review was 45 minutes of teams reading their dashboards out loud. Nobody left with a decision made. We rebuilt it around three questions instead.
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: Three questions, every time
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: Which services burned more than 25% of their error budget this week? What toil showed up more than twice? What runbook or alert got used and turned out to be wrong? Every other topic gets redirected to a different meeting or a written doc. This constraint is what makes the meeting short and the same length every week.
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: Every item leaves with an owner and a date
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: A finding without an owner is a complaint. We stopped accepting "someone should look at this" as an outcome — every item raised gets a named owner and a date before the meeting ends, tracked in the same doc we review the following week. Items that roll over three weeks unaddressed get escalated automatically to the engineering managers, not discussed again in the same meeting.
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: Rotate who presents
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: We rotate which team presents their burn-rate and toil numbers each week rather than having one reliability lead present everyone's data. This forced every team to actually look at their own numbers before the meeting instead of outsourcing that thinking, and it surfaced problems teams hadn't noticed in their own services.
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: Kill the meeting if there's nothing to discuss
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: Some weeks all three questions come back empty — no budget breach, no repeat toil, no wrong runbook. We cancel the meeting outright in that case instead of filling 30 minutes anyway, and send a one-line async note confirming the quiet week. Treating a cancelled meeting as a legitimate, positive outcome — not a missed obligation — was what finally convinced skeptical teams the review wasn't just theater.
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: Fix the agenda to three questions: budget burn, repeat toil, wrong runbooks/alerts.
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: Cap the meeting at 30 minutes and enforce it.
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: Every finding leaves with a named owner and a date, not a vague action item.
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: Rotate presenting teams so ownership of the numbers doesn't concentrate in one role.
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: Cancel the meeting outright on genuinely quiet weeks instead of padding the agenda.
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update
slots.label: Reliability Reviews: The Meeting That Isn't a Status Update

slots.sample: Toil is easy to complain about and hard to measure. We started logging it like an incident, and the pattern that fell out surprised us.
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: Everyone on the rotation agreed toil was a problem. Nobody could say how much, or which task was worst, until we started logging it the same way we log incidents.
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: Log it like you'd log an incident
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: We added a lightweight toil log: task name, time spent, whether it was automatable. Engineers filled it in during the same handoff ritual where they already summarize the shift, so it added roughly 90 seconds, not a new chore. After a quarter we had enough data to rank toil the same way we rank alert noise.
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: The top offender was rarely the loudest complaint
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: The task everyone complained about in Slack — manually rotating a credential — turned out to be 12 minutes a month. The task nobody mentioned — re-running a stuck ETL job by hand — was 6 hours a month across the rotation. Measured data reprioritized the automation backlog completely, and the visible-complaint task stayed manual for another quarter because it genuinely wasn't worth automating yet.
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: Set a toil budget, not just an error budget
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: We now cap toil at 10% of on-call time per rotation member per month, tracked from the same log. Crossing it triggers the same kind of review an error budget breach does — not a punishment, a forcing function to pull an automation task off the backlog before the next cycle.
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: Keep the log honest by making it cheap
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: The first version of the log asked for a category, a severity, and a free-text description, and adoption was terrible within two weeks — filling it in felt like more toil on top of the toil. Cutting it down to a task name picked from a short list and a rough time estimate is what actually got people to keep using it past the novelty period.
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: Log toil with the same rigor as incidents: task, time, automatability.
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: Rank by total time spent, not by how often it's complained about.
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: Set a toil budget per rotation member and review breaches like SLO breaches.
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: Automate the highest total-time offender first, not the loudest one.
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: Keep the logging mechanism cheap or people will quietly stop doing it.
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do
slots.label: Toil Reduction: Measuring the Work Nobody Wants to Do

slots.sample: We deleted 43 alerts in a single afternoon and pager volume dropped 30% overnight. Here is the rule we used to decide what to cut.
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: An alert that has never once led to a real action is not a safety net. It's noise that makes every real page slower to trust.
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: The action-rate rule
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: For every alert that fired more than five times in a quarter, we checked whether the responder's resolution field said anything other than "no action" or "self-resolved." Anything under a 10% action rate got flagged for deletion or demotion to a non-paging channel. This is a mechanical, defensible rule — nobody has to argue in a meeting about whether an alert "feels" useful.
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: Demote before you delete
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: Not every low-action alert is worthless — some are early warnings that are correct to fire even if the fix is rarely urgent. Those got demoted to a dashboard tile or a daily digest instead of a page. Only alerts with zero real actions across the full quarter got deleted outright.
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: Make hygiene a recurring job, not a one-time cleanup
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: The 43-alert cleanup was satisfying but it will rot again if it's a one-time event. We now run the action-rate query on the first Monday of every month as a standing agenda item in the reliability review, so noise gets caught within weeks instead of accumulating for a year.
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: Tell people before you cut
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: We post the candidate deletion list in the team channel 48 hours before acting on it, rather than silently removing alerts the moment the query flags them. Twice this caught an alert that looked useless by the numbers but was actually a known-good check for a rare seasonal failure mode nobody had triggered in the sample window — a heads-up that took thirty seconds saved us from deleting something we'd have badly missed.
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: Compute action rate per alert; anything under 10% is a candidate for change.
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: Demote low-value-but-correct alerts to a dashboard before deleting them outright.
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: Delete only alerts with zero real actions across a full quarter.
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: Announce deletion candidates before acting — some quiet alerts guard rare failures.
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: Re-run the audit monthly — alert rot is continuous, not a one-time cleanup.
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On
slots.label: Alert Hygiene: Deleting the Alerts Nobody Acts On

slots.sample: An error budget policy written during calm times gets renegotiated the moment a big launch is on the line. Here is how we made ours hold.
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: Every error budget policy sounds reasonable in a planning doc. The real test is whether it survives the week before a launch the whole company is counting on.
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: Write exceptions in, not around
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: Our first policy had no exception process, so the first time a launch conflicted with a budget freeze, the team simply ignored the policy and shipped anyway — which taught everyone the policy was optional. The rewrite includes an explicit exception path: a VP can approve a time-boxed, logged override, capped at 14 days, after which the freeze re-applies automatically whether or not anyone remembers to lift it.
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: Automate the trigger, not the decision
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: The freeze condition itself is computed automatically from burn rate, not decided in a meeting — that removes the moment where someone can argue the numbers don't really mean what they say.
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: Make the cost of overriding visible
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: Every override is logged with who approved it, why, and for how long, and that log is reviewed publicly in the monthly reliability review. Visibility, not enforcement, turned out to be what discouraged casual overrides — nobody wants their name on a list of budget exceptions justified by "the roadmap deadline was already announced."
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: Involve product in writing it, not just engineering
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: Our first draft was written entirely by the SRE team and read, to product stakeholders, like an obstacle rather than a shared agreement — which is exactly why it got quietly bypassed the first time it was inconvenient. The rewrite had a product leader co-sign the exception thresholds, and having someone with launch-timeline authority already bought into the policy meant the override conversation during our next big launch took ten minutes instead of a day of escalation.
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: Build an explicit, time-boxed exception path instead of hoping nobody needs one.
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: Compute the freeze trigger automatically from burn rate, not by discussion.
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: Cap overrides and auto-re-apply the freeze when the cap expires.
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: Log every override publicly and review it in the monthly reliability meeting.
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: Co-author the policy with product, not just engineering, so it isn't seen as an obstacle.
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline
slots.label: Writing an Error Budget Policy That Survives a Launch Deadline

slots.sample: A single burn-rate window either pages too late on slow leaks or too eagerly on brief blips. We run two windows at once and it fixed both problems.
slots.label: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts: Fast and Slow, Together

slots.sample: A single-window burn-rate alert forces an uncomfortable tradeoff: a short window catches fast burns but flaps on noise, a long window is stable but misses the incident until half your budget is already gone.
slots.label: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts: Fast and Slow, Together

slots.sample: Why one window isn't enough
slots.label: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts: Fast and Slow, Together

slots.sample: We initially alerted on a 1-hour window at 14x burn rate — sensitive enough to catch outages fast, but it also fired on five-minute blips that self-resolved before anyone could act. Widening to a 6-hour window fixed the flapping but meant we sometimes didn't page until 35% of the monthly budget was already spent on a slow, steady degradation.
slots.label: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts: Fast and Slow, Together

slots.sample: Two windows, one alert
slots.label: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts: Fast and Slow, Together

slots.sample: We now require both a fast window and a slow window to agree before paging: a short window confirms the burn is real right now, a long window confirms it isn't a blip. This is the standard multi-window, multi-burn-rate pattern, and it cut false pages by more than half while catching slow burns days earlier than the single long window did on its own.
slots.label: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts: Fast and Slow, Together

slots.sample: Tune thresholds from budget math, not gut feel
slots.label: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts: Fast and Slow, Together

slots.sample: The burn-rate multipliers aren't arbitrary — they're derived from how much budget a sustained burn at that rate would consume in the alert's window relative to the SLO period. We keep a small reference table per service so new SLOs get sane starting thresholds instead of everyone re-deriving the math from scratch.
slots.label: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts: Fast and Slow, Together

slots.sample: A short window for recovery, too
slots.label: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts: Fast and Slow, Together

slots.sample: The same fast window that confirms a burn is real also tells us when it's over — once the short window drops back under threshold while the long window is still elevated, we downgrade the page to a lower-urgency notification instead of leaving it open at full severity. That distinction between "still actively burning" and "recovering but budget already spent" changes what the responder should be doing next.
slots.label: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts: Fast and Slow, Together

slots.sample: Never page on a single burn-rate window alone — pair a fast and a slow window.
slots.label: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts: Fast and Slow, Together

slots.sample: Require both windows to agree before triggering the page.
slots.label: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts: Fast and Slow, Together

slots.sample: Derive burn-rate multipliers from budget math, not intuition.
slots.label: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts: Fast and Slow, Together

slots.sample: Keep a per-service threshold reference table so new SLOs start from a sane default.
slots.label: Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerts: Fast and Slow, Together

slots.sample: Downgrade severity once the fast window recovers, even if the slow window is still elevated.

slots.sample: We stopped scheduling a two-hour SLO workshop for every new service and replaced it with a self-serve template that gets a defensible target in 20 minutes.
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: Setting an SLO used to mean booking a room with six people for two hours to argue about a number nobody had data for yet. We built a self-serve path instead.
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: Start with a template query, not a blank page
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: Every new service gets a starter HelixQL query that computes what its SLI would have been over the last 30 days, using traffic that already exists. Nobody has to invent a target from nothing — they see a real historical number first and adjust from there.
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: Publish a default, let teams override with reasons
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: We set a sane organizational default — 99.5% availability, 500ms p95 latency — as the starting SLO for anything without a stated business reason to differ. Teams that want a tighter or looser target write one paragraph explaining why, attached to the SLO definition. This removed the meeting entirely for about 70% of new services; only the genuinely unusual ones need a discussion.
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: Review, don't relitigate, at 90 days
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: Instead of a live workshop, the 90-day review is a written comment thread on the SLO doc: has the target been consistently missed, consistently trivial to hit, or about right? Two of the three outcomes require a change; the third requires nothing, which is most of the time.
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: Keep a human escape hatch for the genuinely unusual
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: A handful of services really do need the room full of people — a payments-adjacent service with regulatory latency requirements, for instance, isn't well served by a generic default. The self-serve path has an explicit "this doesn't fit" button that books a proper workshop, and using it isn't treated as a failure of the async process, just an acknowledgment that some SLOs are genuinely more complicated than a template can handle.
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: Compute a starter SLI value from real historical traffic before setting any target.
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: Publish a sane organizational default and require a written reason to deviate.
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: Replace live SLO workshops with an async written review at 90 days.
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: Only escalate to a meeting when the async review can't reach a decision.
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: Keep an explicit escape hatch to a real workshop for genuinely unusual services.
slots.label: SLOs Without Meetings: Setting Targets From Data, Not a War Room

slots.sample: Standing up a new team's first rotation is where most of the bad habits get baked in permanently. Here is the checklist we now use on day one.
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: A rotation's worst habits are set in its first month and are brutally hard to unwind later. We built a day-one checklist after fixing three rotations that had already calcified badly.
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: Size it from expected page volume, not headcount you have
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: We estimate expected weekly pages from comparable services before deciding rotation size, rather than just splitting whoever is on the team evenly. A team of four with an expected two pages a week doesn't need a formal secondary shift yet; a team of four expecting fifteen does, even if that means borrowing responders from an adjacent team temporarily.
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: Set the escalation policy before the first page, not after
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: New rotations often discover their escalation policy is wrong during the first real incident, which is the worst possible time. We now require a documented, tested escalation chain — including a named backup for the backup — before a service goes on a paging rotation at all, and we test it with a synthetic page in business hours before it ever fires for real.
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: Budget onboarding time into the first shift
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: A new engineer's first on-call shift should not be their first exposure to the runbooks. We pair a new responder with a shadow shift — full visibility into pages, zero responsibility to act — before their first solo shift. Skipping this step was the single biggest predictor of a bad first incident in the rotations we audited.
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: Write the rotation's first retro before the first incident
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: We schedule a 30-day rotation retro on the calendar the same day the rotation goes live, before there's necessarily anything dramatic to discuss. Waiting for a bad incident to justify a retro means the small annoyances — a confusing dashboard link, an alert that fires slightly too eager — never get raised until they've compounded into something that actually hurts.
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: Size the rotation from expected page volume of comparable services, not headcount.
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: Document and test the full escalation chain before the first real page.
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: Require a shadow shift before anyone's first solo on-call rotation.
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: Schedule the first rotation retro on day one, not after something goes wrong.
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: Revisit rotation size after the first quarter of real page data.
slots.label: Building a Sane On-Call Rotation From Scratch

slots.sample: You don't need a quarter-long project to find your worst alerts. A single HelixQL query and an afternoon is enough to find where to start.
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: Teams keep telling us alert cleanup is a multi-week project. Ours took an afternoon, because the hard part was never the analysis — it was deciding to look.
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: One query, ranked two ways
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: We ranked every alert two ways in the same query: by raw fire count, and by fire count weighted against action rate. The first ranking tells you what's loud. The second tells you what's actually worth fixing — an alert that fires 200 times and gets acted on 190 of them is healthy noise; one that fires 200 times and gets acted on 3 is the real target.
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: Fifteen alerts, not fifty
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: We capped the audit at the top 15 by weighted score rather than trying to review every alert in the system. That constraint is what made it fit in an afternoon — the long tail of low-volume alerts genuinely isn't worth a team's attention in a single sitting, and chasing it is how these projects balloon into a quarter.
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: Assign one fix each, due before the next audit
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: Every alert in the top 15 leaves the meeting with exactly one assigned action: delete, demote, or fix the underlying threshold. We schedule the next audit for 30 days out on the calendar before the meeting ends, which is what actually makes the second audit happen.
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: Bring the query, not a pre-made slide deck
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: We run the query live in the meeting instead of presenting a static export from last week. Alert data moves fast enough that a five-day-old snapshot has already drifted, and running it live also means anyone in the room can suggest a filter tweak on the spot — narrowing to one team's services, say — without waiting for someone to regenerate a deck.
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: Rank alerts by fire count weighted against action rate, not raw volume alone.
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: Cap the review at the top 10–15 alerts to fit in a single afternoon.
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: Assign one concrete action per alert — delete, demote, or fix — before the meeting ends.
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: Run the query live in the meeting rather than presenting a stale export.
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: Schedule the next audit immediately so it actually recurs.
slots.label: The Pager Audit: Three Months of Alerts in One Afternoon

slots.sample: A runbook is a snapshot of a system that keeps changing. Here is how we catch the moment a documented fix stops matching reality.
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: We found a runbook telling engineers to SSH into a box that had been decommissioned four months earlier. Nobody had noticed because nobody had needed that runbook since.
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: Link runbooks to the services they describe
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: Every runbook now references a service ID in the service catalog. When that service's infrastructure changes in a way we track — a host migration, a queue replacement, a major dependency swap — the linked runbooks get automatically flagged as needing review instead of silently drifting.
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: Verify by running, not by reading
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: A reviewer re-reading a runbook and nodding along is not verification — they're pattern-matching that it sounds plausible. Real verification means running the confirmation query and, where safe, the first remediation step against a staging environment on a schedule.
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: Archive aggressively
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: A stale runbook is worse than no runbook, because it gets followed with false confidence during an incident. We archive anything unverified for 180 days rather than letting it linger — an archived runbook that turns out to still be needed gets restored and re-verified in minutes; a rotted one followed blindly costs a lot more.
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: Assign verification to whoever changed the system
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: Instead of routing every flagged runbook back to its original author, who may have left the team or the company by the time it drifts, we route the re-verification task to whoever made the infrastructure change that triggered the flag. They already have the context on what's different, and it spreads runbook ownership across the team naturally instead of concentrating it on whoever happened to write the first draft two years ago.
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: Link every runbook to a service ID so infrastructure changes trigger a review flag.
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: Verify by actually running the confirmation query and safe steps, not by re-reading.
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: Track days-since-verified as a first-class metric, reviewed monthly.
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: Route re-verification to whoever made the triggering change, not always the original author.
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: Archive anything unverified past 180 days rather than letting it rot in place.
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale
slots.label: Runbook Rot: Keeping Procedures From Going Stale

slots.sample: Legacy services without a clear owner are exactly where SLOs matter most and get skipped most often. Here is how we forced the question.
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: Our internal notification service had no SLO, no clear owner, and three teams that each assumed someone else was watching it — until it caused a two-hour outage nobody was paged for.
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: Ownership gaps show up in the paging data first
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: Before assigning an SLO, we ran a simple query to find services with real traffic and zero linked on-call rotation. That gap list became the starting point for a forced ownership conversation, because you can't set a meaningful SLO for a service where nobody would be paged if it breached one.
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: Default to the most demanding dependent
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: For services with unclear ownership but clear dependents, we set the initial SLO to match the tightest requirement among the services that depend on it, not a generic default. If checkout depends on notification-service and checkout needs 99.9%, notification-service inherits at least that bar until someone actively renegotiates it — the default should make under-protection the exception, not the norm.
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: Assign a temporary owner with an expiration date
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: We stopped waiting for a permanent owner to be resolved through an org-design process before adding paging. A temporary owning team is assigned with a 60-day expiration, after which either a real owner has been found or it escalates to engineering leadership automatically — this turned an indefinitely stalled conversation into one with a forcing function.
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: Don't let the temporary owner become permanent by default
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: The obvious failure mode is that the temporary team just keeps the service forever because nobody revisits it — we had exactly this happen once before adding a hard rule. The 60-day expiration is a real calendar event, not a soft target, and it forces an explicit yes-or-no: does this team formally take ownership, or does it get reassigned. Silence resolves to escalation, never to quiet permanence.
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: Find ownerless services by joining traffic volume against rotation coverage.
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: Default an unowned service's SLO to its most demanding dependent's requirement.
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: Assign a temporary owner with a hard expiration rather than waiting for consensus.
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: Escalate automatically to leadership if ownership is still unresolved at expiration.
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: Never let a temporary owner become permanent by default silence.
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own
slots.label: Setting an SLO for a Service Nobody Agreed to Own

slots.sample: Too little headroom and a normal traffic spike becomes an incident. Too much and you're burning budget on idle capacity. We found a number that works for us.
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: "Add more headroom" is not a capacity plan. We needed an actual number, derived from how spiky our real traffic is, not a round figure someone picked once.
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: Derive headroom from your actual spike ratio
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: We computed the ratio of our worst sustained 15-minute peak to our typical weekday average over the last two quarters, per service, instead of applying a flat 30% headroom rule everywhere. Some services spike 1.4x average; our billing-webhook consumer spikes 6x during month-end batch runs. One headroom number was never going to fit both.
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: Headroom is a moving target, not a one-time budget line
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: We recompute spike ratio quarterly rather than setting capacity once at launch and forgetting it. A service that grows its user base gradually can see its spike ratio shift meaningfully within two quarters, and capacity that was generous at launch becomes tight without any single dramatic change to notice.
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: Alert on headroom shrinking, not just on saturation
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: By the time a saturation alert fires, you're already out of runway. We added a second, quieter alert that fires when the gap between current peak usage and provisioned capacity drops below 20%, giving the team weeks of lead time to provision instead of hours.
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: Price the headroom, don't just provision it
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: Extra capacity isn't free, and treating headroom as a purely technical decision hides its real cost from the people who'd want to weigh in on it. We now attach an estimated monthly cost to each service's headroom target next to its spike ratio, so a request to raise a target from 40% to 80% is visibly also a request for a specific dollar figure, not an abstract safety margin nobody has to account for.
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: Derive headroom per service from its actual peak-to-typical spike ratio.
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: Recompute the ratio quarterly — it drifts with organic growth.
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: Alert on shrinking headroom, not only on saturation itself.
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: Attach an estimated cost to headroom targets so the tradeoff is visible.
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: Treat a flat, org-wide headroom percentage as a starting guess, not a final answer.
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough
slots.label: Capacity Headroom: How Much Slack Is Enough

slots.sample: Not every toil task is worth automating. We built a simple return-on-effort filter before greenlighting any automation project.
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: Engineers love automating things. Not every toil task deserves it — some cost more to automate safely than they'll ever save. We needed a filter before approving the backlog.
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: Compute payback period before writing code
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: For each candidate task we estimate engineering hours to automate against monthly hours saved, from the toil log, and compute a payback period in months. Anything with a payback under six months gets greenlit by default; anything over eighteen needs an explicit justification beyond time saved, like reducing error rate or removing a single-point-of-failure person.
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: Automate the boring 80%, keep a human in the risky 20%
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: Full automation of a task is often far more effort than partial automation, for a fraction of the benefit. Our credential-rotation toil task didn't need a fully automated pipeline — a script that does the mechanical 80% and hands a human a two-click approval for the risky part cut the time by 90% at a fraction of the build cost of full automation.
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: Track whether automation actually held up
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: We revisit automated tasks 90 days after shipping to confirm the toil actually disappeared from the log, rather than assuming the project succeeded because it shipped. A few of our early automations quietly reintroduced manual steps within weeks because an edge case wasn't handled, and we wouldn't have caught it without checking the log again.
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: Let the person who does the toil pick the filter's inputs
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: Engineering estimates of build effort tend to run optimistic, and toil-log time estimates tend to run conservative, so we have the responder who actually performs the task review both numbers before a payback calculation gets approved. Letting the estimate come only from whoever's excited to build the automation reliably produced payback periods that looked better on paper than they turned out to be in practice.
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: Compute a payback period in months before approving any automation project.
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: Prefer partial automation with a human checkpoint over full automation of risky steps.
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: Justify automations with an 18+ month payback on non-time grounds explicitly.
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: Have the person doing the toil review both the effort and time-saved estimates.
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: Re-check the toil log 90 days post-launch to confirm the win actually held.
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify
slots.label: Cutting Toil With Automation You Can Actually Justify

slots.sample: Not every alert deserves to interrupt someone's night. We rebuilt our routing rules around actual urgency instead of defaulting everything to a page.
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: We were paging our on-call engineer at 2 a.m. for issues that could safely wait until business hours. That's not diligence, it's a design failure in the routing layer.
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: Classify by real urgency, not by source
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: Every alert used to route to a page by default unless someone remembered to configure otherwise, which meant urgency was decided by omission. We flipped the default: every new alert starts as a non-paging notification, and only alerts explicitly tied to user-facing impact or SLO burn get promoted to paging, reviewed at creation time.
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: Time-of-day aware routing for genuinely borderline alerts
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: A handful of alerts are urgent during business hours but tolerable overnight — a batch job running slow, for instance, matters far less at 3 a.m. than at 9 a.m. when people are waiting on its output. Those route to a page during business hours and to a digest queue overnight, reviewed first thing by whoever starts their day next.
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: Measure interrupted sleep as its own metric
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: We now track pages that fire between 11 p.m. and 6 a.m. local time to the responder as a distinct number from total page volume. Overall pages can go down while overnight pages stay flat if you're not watching this specifically — and overnight pages are the ones that actually drive burnout and attrition.
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: Respect local time, not server time
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: Our first pass at this used UTC cutoffs across a rotation that spans three time zones, which meant "overnight" for one responder was mid-afternoon for another and the routing rules were silently wrong for two-thirds of the team. Routing now resolves against each responder's actual local time at the moment of the page, which sounds obvious in hindsight but took a real bug report to notice.
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: Default new alerts to non-paging; require an explicit reason to promote to a page.
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: Use time-of-day aware routing for alerts that are urgent by day but tolerable overnight.
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: Track overnight pages as a distinct metric from total page volume.
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: Resolve overnight windows against each responder's local time, not server time.
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: Review alerts that page without a linked SLO — that's usually a routing mistake.
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep
slots.label: Alert Routing That Respects Sleep

slots.sample: We had three people who could run a major incident and eleven who could not. Here is how we built a pipeline instead of a bottleneck.
slots.label: Training the Second Seat: Growing More Incident Commanders

slots.sample: Every serious incident routed to the same three people, because they were the only ones trusted to run it. That's not resilience, that's a single point of failure with a badge that says incident commander.
slots.label: Training the Second Seat: Growing More Incident Commanders

slots.sample: Shadow before you solo
slots.label: Training the Second Seat: Growing More Incident Commanders

slots.sample: We introduced a formal second-seat role: a trainee IC sits in on every declared incident above a certain severity, observes decisions in real time, and debriefs with the acting IC afterward without any responsibility for the outcome. This removed the all-or-nothing jump from zero incident experience to owning a live one.
slots.label: Training the Second Seat: Growing More Incident Commanders

slots.sample: Run drills on real, closed incidents
slots.label: Training the Second Seat: Growing More Incident Commanders

slots.sample: We replay a past incident's timeline with the trainee as IC and the original responders roleplaying their parts, using the actual burn-rate query and timeline data from the real event. It's realistic without the stakes, and gives us a query we can point trainees at directly.
slots.label: Training the Second Seat: Growing More Incident Commanders

slots.sample: Make it a track, not a favor
slots.label: Training the Second Seat: Growing More Incident Commanders

slots.sample: IC training used to happen informally, whoever a senior engineer decided to mentor. slots.sample: Our first SLI was 100% green while users were filing complaints. The gap taught us to stop measuring what was easy and start measuring what mattered.
slots.label: SLIs That Measure What Users Actually Feel

slots.sample: We had a beautiful 99.97% availability SLI and a support queue full of angry users during the exact window it claimed was healthy. The SLI was measuring the wrong thing.
slots.label: SLIs That Measure What Users Actually Feel

slots.sample: Server success is not the same as user success
slots.label: SLIs That Measure What Users Actually Feel

slots.sample: Our original SLI counted a request as "good" if the server returned a 2xx status code. It didn't catch a client-side bug where the checkout button silently failed to submit after a successful API call — technically a server success, functionally a broken checkout. We rewrote the SLI to include the full user-facing outcome, not just the backend response.
slots.label: SLIs That Measure What Users Actually Feel

slots.sample: Validate against a channel users actually use
slots.label: SLIs That Measure What Users Actually Feel

slots.sample: We cross-checked our new SLI against support ticket volume for the same period, rather than trusting the new definition just because it felt more thorough. When the SLI dipped, ticket volume should rise within the hour; when it didn't correlate, that told us the SLI still had a gap, and we iterated twice more before the two lined up consistently.
slots.label: SLIs That Measure What Users Actually Feel

slots.sample: Accept that some SLIs need synthetic checks, not just real traffic
slots.label: SLIs That Measure What Users Actually Feel

slots.sample: For low-traffic but high-importance paths — password reset, for instance — real traffic volume is too sparse to compute a meaningful rolling SLI. We layered in synthetic checks that exercise the flow every few minutes specifically to keep the SLI statistically meaningful even during quiet hours.
slots.label: SLIs That Measure What Users Actually Feel

slots.sample: Let support flag SLI gaps, not just confirm them
slots.label: SLIs That Measure What Users Actually Feel

slots.sample: Beyond validating the SLI after the fact, we now give the support team a lightweight way to tag a ticket as "the dashboards said we were fine" directly, which routes straight to the SLI owner instead of getting lost in a general feedback backlog. That direct channel caught a second gap — a subtly broken retry path — faster than any scheduled review would have.
slots.label: SLIs That Measure What Users Actually Feel

slots.sample: Define "good" as the full user-facing outcome, not just the backend response code.
slots.label: SLIs That Measure What Users Actually Feel

slots.sample: Validate a new SLI against an independent signal like support ticket volume.
slots.label: SLIs That Measure What Users Actually Feel

slots.sample: Iterate the SLI definition until it actually correlates with user pain, not once.
slots.label: SLIs That Measure What Users Actually Feel

slots.sample: Add synthetic checks for low-traffic, high-importance paths.

slots.sample: "More people" is the default answer to a painful rotation, but it's often the wrong one. Here is the actual formula we use before headcount conversations.
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: Every painful rotation conversation eventually turns into a headcount request. Before we make that ask, we run the numbers, because sometimes the fix is shift length, not people.
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: The variables that actually matter
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: Rotation size should be driven by three inputs: expected pages per week, acceptable pages per person per shift, and desired shift length. We derive minimum headcount from those, rather than starting from whatever the team happens to be staffed at.
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: Shift length changes the answer more than headcount does
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: For a team receiving 12 pages a week with a target of at most 4 pages per person per week-long shift, the math says you need 3 people. Cut the shift to 3.5 days instead and recompute — the per-shift page count drops proportionally, and the same 3 people now experience a lighter, shorter burden without adding a fourth person to the rotation at all.
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: Use the math to make the ask, not avoid it
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: Sometimes the math genuinely says you need more people, and having the formula makes that request concrete and hard to argue with — "we need 5, we have 3, here's the query and the assumptions" lands very differently than "on-call is rough lately." The goal isn't to avoid headcount asks, it's to make them evidence-based.
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: Watch for the formula being technically satisfied but still painful
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: A rotation can hit every number in the formula and still feel bad if the pages are unevenly distributed across the week — five quiet nights and two brutal ones average out to a comfortable number that nobody actually experiences. We pair the headcount formula with a variance check across days of the week before declaring a rotation healthy on paper.
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: Derive rotation size from expected pages, target pages-per-shift, and shift length.
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: Try shortening shift length before defaulting to a headcount request.
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: Recompute the formula quarterly as page volume changes.
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: Check variance across days, not just the average — a healthy average can hide bad days.
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: When the math says you need more people, use it to make the ask concrete.
slots.label: The On-Call Rotation Math: How Many Engineers Do You Need

slots.sample: We almost migrated everything to burn-rate alerting and dropped every static threshold. A near-miss taught us why both still earn a place.
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: Burn-rate alerting felt like a strict upgrade over static thresholds, so we started migrating everything. A near-miss with a slow memory leak stopped us halfway through.
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: What burn-rate alerts are bad at
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: Burn-rate alerts are tied to an SLO window, which means they're blind to problems that haven't yet produced enough bad events to move the ratio — a memory leak climbing steadily toward an OOM kill produces zero SLI-visible badness until the moment it crosses the line and takes the service down all at once. A static threshold on memory usage would have caught it hours earlier.
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: What static thresholds are bad at
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: Static thresholds don't know what's actually SLO-relevant, so they either page on things that don't matter to users or need constant hand-tuning as normal usage patterns shift with traffic growth. We keep them for leading-indicator, cause-based signals — memory, disk, queue depth — and use burn rate for anything measuring actual user-facing impact.
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: The dividing line we settled on
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: If the signal directly represents user experience, it becomes a burn-rate alert against an SLO. If it's a leading indicator that predicts future user impact before it happens, it stays a static or trend-based threshold, usually routed to a non-paging channel unless it's climbing fast. Neither approach replaces the other; they cover different failure shapes.
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: Document the pairing per service, not just in principle
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: Every service's alert catalog now lists its burn-rate alerts and its leading-indicator thresholds side by side, with a one-line note on what failure each one is meant to catch. That forced us to notice two services that had burn-rate coverage but no leading indicators at all — the exact gap that caused the near-miss in the first place — and fix them before they repeated it.
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: Use burn-rate alerts for anything that directly measures user-facing impact.
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: Keep static or trend thresholds for leading indicators like memory and queue depth.
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: Don't migrate everything to burn rate — it's blind to problems before they hit the SLI.
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: Route leading-indicator alerts to a non-paging channel unless they're climbing fast.
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: Document both alert types per service so gaps in the pairing are easy to spot.
slots.label: Burn Rate Alerts vs. Threshold Alerts: Why You Need Both

slots.sample: Our capacity planning used to be a two-week spreadsheet exercise every quarter. We replaced most of it with a query that runs in seconds.
slots.label: Quarterly Capacity Planning Without the Spreadsheet Marathon

slots.sample: Capacity planning ate two weeks of an engineer's quarter, manually exporting metrics into a spreadsheet and eyeballing growth trends. Almost none of that work needed a human.
slots.label: Quarterly Capacity Planning Without the Spreadsheet Marathon

slots.sample: Automate the growth projection
slots.label: Quarterly Capacity Planning Without the Spreadsheet Marathon

slots.sample: We compute trailing growth rate per service directly from telemetry and project it forward, rather than having someone manually chart request volume in a spreadsheet every quarter. The query produces the same projection a careful analyst would, in seconds instead of days, and it's reproducible the same way every time.
slots.label: Quarterly Capacity Planning Without the Spreadsheet Marathon

slots.sample: Reserve human time for the exceptions
slots.label: Quarterly Capacity Planning Without the Spreadsheet Marathon

slots.sample: The automated projection is right most of the time and wrong in interesting ways for services with known upcoming changes — a marketing campaign, a new integration partner, a planned deprecation. We spend the time we saved reviewing only the outliers and the services flagged with an upcoming known event, not re-deriving numbers the query already gets right.
slots.label: Quarterly Capacity Planning Without the Spreadsheet Marathon

slots.sample: Tie the output directly to a provisioning decision
slots.label: Quarterly Capacity Planning Without the Spreadsheet Marathon

slots.sample: A projection that doesn't lead to a decision is just a chart. Every service with projected growth above its current headroom threshold automatically generates a provisioning ticket with the target date attached, so the loop from "we noticed" to "we acted" doesn't depend on someone remembering to follow up after the planning meeting.
slots.label: Quarterly Capacity Planning Without the Spreadsheet Marathon

slots.sample: Keep last quarter's projection visible next to this quarter's
slots.label: Quarterly Capacity Planning Without the Spreadsheet Marathon

slots.sample: We display the prior quarter's forecast alongside the new one so anyone reviewing can see at a glance how accurate the model actually was, not just what it predicts now. A service that consistently over- or under-shoots its own projection is telling you something about its growth pattern — usually that it's lumpy rather than linear — and that's a signal worth a human look even when the current quarter's number seems unremarkable.
slots.label: Quarterly Capacity Planning Without the Spreadsheet Marathon

slots.sample: Compute trailing growth rate and forward projection directly from telemetry.
slots.label: Quarterly Capacity Planning Without the Spreadsheet Marathon

slots.sample: Spend human review time only on flagged exceptions and known upcoming events.
slots.label: Quarterly Capacity Planning Without the Spreadsheet Marathon

slots.sample: Auto-generate a provisioning ticket when projected growth exceeds current headroom.
slots.label: Quarterly Capacity Planning Without the Spreadsheet Marathon

slots.sample: A freeze that never actually triggers isn't a policy, it's decoration. We tracked ours for a year to see if it meant anything.
slots.label: The Error Budget Freeze: When to Actually Pull the Brake

slots.sample: We wrote an error budget freeze policy a year ago and then quietly wondered whether it had ever actually stopped anyone from shipping anything.
slots.label: The Error Budget Freeze: When to Actually Pull the Brake

slots.sample: Audit whether the freeze ever bites
slots.label: The Error Budget Freeze: When to Actually Pull the Brake

slots.sample: We pulled every week in the last year where a service crossed its freeze threshold and checked whether any deploy to that service was actually blocked or delayed as a result. In four of eleven qualifying weeks, deploys went out anyway with no recorded exception — meaning the policy was being silently ignored, not overridden through the proper process.
slots.label: The Error Budget Freeze: When to Actually Pull the Brake

slots.sample: Make the freeze technically enforced, not just documented
slots.label: The Error Budget Freeze: When to Actually Pull the Brake

slots.sample: A policy that depends on everyone remembering and choosing to comply will eventually get skipped under deadline pressure, exactly when it matters most. We wired the freeze state into the deploy pipeline itself — a frozen service requires an explicit, logged override flag to deploy at all, rather than trusting a Slack announcement to be read and honored.
slots.label: The Error Budget Freeze: When to Actually Pull the Brake

slots.sample: Review freeze frequency, not just freeze compliance
slots.label: The Error Budget Freeze: When to Actually Pull the Brake

slots.sample: A service that freezes every single month isn't disciplined, it's chronically over budget, which is a different problem than a policy-compliance problem. We now flag services with three or more freezes in a rolling six months for a deeper reliability investment conversation, separate from the weekly freeze-compliance check.
slots.label: The Error Budget Freeze: When to Actually Pull the Brake

slots.sample: Give the override a real cost, not just a log entry
slots.label: The Error Budget Freeze: When to Actually Pull the Brake

slots.sample: Logging an override is necessary but not sufficient — we found that once a service had overridden its freeze once, doing it a second time felt easier, and a third time felt routine. We added a rule that a second override within the same 30-day window requires sign-off from a director rather than a VP, which raised the friction just enough to make the second ask genuinely deliberate instead of a rubber stamp.
slots.label: The Error Budget Freeze: When to Actually Pull the Brake

slots.sample: Audit whether your freeze policy has ever actually blocked a deploy — don't assume.
slots.label: The Error Budget Freeze: When to Actually Pull the Brake

slots.sample: Wire the freeze into the deploy pipeline technically, not just as a documented rule.
slots.label: The Error Budget Freeze: When to Actually Pull the Brake

slots.sample: Require a logged override flag for any deploy to a frozen service.
slots.label: The Error Budget Freeze: When to Actually Pull the Brake

slots.sample: Escalate the approval bar for repeat overrides within the same window.
slots.label: The Error Budget Freeze: When to Actually Pull the Brake

slots.sample: A bad escalation policy either pages a whole team for a minor issue or leaves a major incident unstaffed while primary sleeps through it. We rebuilt ours around severity.
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: Twice in one month our escalation policy failed in opposite directions: once it paged four people for a blip, once it let a genuine outage sit unstaffed for twenty minutes because primary's phone was on silent.
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: Escalate on missed acknowledgment, tied to severity
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: Low-severity alerts wait a full 10 minutes before escalating past primary, giving room for someone mid-task to notice and acknowledge. High-severity alerts tied to SLO burn escalate after 3 minutes and notify secondary in parallel rather than sequentially, because those extra minutes of an unstaffed critical incident cost more than the risk of a slightly redundant page.
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: Don't escalate to a whole team by default
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: Our old policy's fallback for any missed acknowledgment was paging the entire team channel, which trained people to assume someone else would answer and made acknowledgment slower, not faster, over time. We replaced that with a strict, ordered chain — primary, then secondary, then the engineering manager — and reserved whole-team paging for a small, explicit list of the highest-severity scenarios.
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: Test escalation chains the way you test failover
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: We schedule a quarterly synthetic escalation test — a fake page that's designed to go unacknowledged by primary on purpose — to confirm secondary actually receives it within the expected window. Two of these tests caught a misconfigured phone number and an expired push-notification token that would otherwise have failed silently during a real incident.
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: Keep the chain current when people change roles
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: An escalation chain is only as good as the roster behind it, and rosters drift constantly — someone changes teams, someone goes on leave, someone's phone number changes and nobody thinks to update the paging tool. We tied the escalation chain to the same identity system that manages team membership, so a role change updates the chain automatically instead of relying on someone remembering a second system exists.
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: Tie escalation timing to severity — critical alerts escalate faster and in parallel.
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: Replace default whole-team paging with a strict, ordered escalation chain.
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: Reserve whole-team paging for a small, explicit set of highest-severity scenarios.
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: Run a quarterly synthetic escalation test to catch silent failures in the chain.
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: Tie the chain to your identity/team-membership system so role changes update it automatically.
slots.label: Escalation Policies That Do Not Wake the Wrong Person

slots.sample: Deleting an alert feels riskier than adding one, so most teams never do it. A small, repeatable ritual made it routine instead of scary.
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep

slots.sample: Nobody wants to be the person who deleted the alert that would have caught the next big outage. That fear is why alert graveyards never actually get cleaned up — until we made retirement a ritual instead of a judgment call.
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep

slots.sample: Demote before you delete, always
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep

slots.sample: No alert goes straight from paging to gone. It first moves to a silent, logged-only state for two weeks, so if it would have fired during that window, we know exactly what we'd have missed before committing to the deletion. This single step is what made engineers comfortable retiring alerts they'd been afraid to touch for years.
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep

slots.sample: Require a one-line reason, logged permanently
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep

slots.sample: Every retired alert keeps a permanent, searchable record of why it was retired and who approved it, even after the alert definition itself is gone. This isn't bureaucracy for its own sake — six months later, when someone asks "didn't we used to alert on this?", the answer is a two-second lookup instead of an afternoon of git archaeology.
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep

slots.sample: Celebrate the deletion, not just the addition
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep

slots.sample: We started including alert retirements in the same weekly update where we announce new dashboards and features, treating a well-justified deletion as a genuine improvement rather than something to quietly do and never mention. That framing shift did more to unstick the backlog of zombie alerts than any process change.
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep

slots.sample: Make the first retirement someone else's, not your own
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep

slots.sample: The very first alert we ever retired under this ritual belonged to the engineer proposing the process, specifically so nobody could accuse the ritual of being a way to dodge accountability for someone else's alert. Leading with your own noisy alert, in public, did more to make the process feel fair than any amount of explaining the safeguards would have.
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep

slots.sample: Demote to silent, logged-only for two weeks before permanently deleting any alert.
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep

slots.sample: Confirm nothing would have fired during the silent period before committing.
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep

slots.sample: Keep a permanent, searchable record of why every alert was retired.
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep

slots.sample: Treat alert retirement as a visible win, not a quiet, risky chore.
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep

slots.sample: Have the process's proposer retire their own alert first to build trust in it.
slots.label: Retiring an Alert: A Short Ritual That Saves a Lot of Sleep
